entries.title: The Rev. Michael Pfleger reinstated at St. Sabina Church after being cleared of child sex abuse claim
entries.summary: <p>The Rev. Michael Pfleger was reinstated in his position as priest at St. Sabina Catholic Church in Auburn Gresham following an investigation into child sex abuse claims against him from decades ago, the Archdiocese of Chicago announced Monday.</p><p>In July, Pfleger was accused of sexually abusing a girl who was a student at St. Sabina sometime between 1993 and 1995. It was the fifth similar accusation against Pfleger within five years. He staunchly denied the most recent accusation as the archdiocese's Independent Review Board investigated.</p><p>The archdiocese said the investigation concluded "there is no reason to believe Father Pfleger is guilty of this allegation."</p><p>"I want to recognize the suffering you and Father Mike have endured, for I know his absence has been real and painful. But I ask you to allow God’s Word this weekend to free you from any sadness and disappointment," Cardinal Blase Cupich said in the statement.</p><p>Cupich praised the investigation process and encouraged parishioners to look to their faith for support as they process Pfleger's absence.</p><p>"In short, no one should underestimate the value of an independent and disciplined inquiry, even if it is made public and requires a substantial amount of time," he wrote.</p><p>Pfleger posted his appreciation on Facebook, accompanied by a link to the archdiocese's statement and a photo of Michael Jordan captioned "I'm back."</p><p>"Thank you God and thanks to all who stood by me," Pfleger wrote.</p><p>After the accusation surfaced in July, some parish leaders called for an overhaul of its abuse investigation process, pushing for a more balanced approach that provides due process for the accused while protecting survivors of abuse. </p><p>Some of the demands from St. Sabina leaders included:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-c07373c2-a022-11f1-acc5-9504bfb668bd"><li>More transparency about investigation timelines and procedures.</li><li>Quicker resolutions to cases.</li><li>Independent review of allegations.</li><li>A tiered suspension policy that would consider factors such as the age of an allegation and whether there is an ongoing risk to children.</li></ul><p>Pfleger has been at the now predominantly Black Catholic church since 1981. He has since become a South Side staple in activism and community work.</p>
entries.author: Mary Norkol

entries.title: Jose Urquidy struggles and departs early as immediate future of White Sox rotation remains murky
entries.summary: <p>After entering behind an opener and flummoxing Cubs hitters for six scoreless innings on just 68 pitches last week, White Sox right-hander <b>José Urquidy</b>’s first start since 2023 saw him use 65 just to get through the top of the second.</p><p>Without command of his changeup, Urquidy walked four and lacked an out-pitch with which to put away Rangers’ hitters, departing after three innings and five runs allowed. A Sox bullpen that already leads MLB in innings–partially due to all the openers <b>Will Venable</b> uses–was tasked with picking up the final six frames, while the future of the team’s rotation remains muddled.</p><p><b>Davis Martin</b> will throw another bullpen on Tuesday before heading out for a rehab start, as he works back from a blister on his middle finger, so he won’t be an option to replace anyone for at least another turn. <b>Erick Fedde </b>has been adequate for 4-5 innings when used behind an opener, but the Sox quickly moved him to relief when the opportunity arose at the start of August. <b>Drew Thorpe</b> is scheduled for another Triple-A rehab start Tuesday, but the Sox haven’t spoken decisively about his future role.</p><p>They have been more clear about expecting <b>Noah Schultz</b> to return from his demotion and make starts down the stretch of their playoff chase. But neither of Schultz’s last two starts with the Knights have exceeded 50 pitches, as the Sox monitor the 22-year-old’s innings.</p><p>“It's part of managing the entire, comprehensive workload for him this year,” Venable said. “At the same time, he's got to pitch and get back to form and accomplish some of the things that he's working on.”</p><p><b>Top prospect gets a new glove</b></p><p>Vaunted third base prospect<b> Caleb Bonemer</b> will receive reps in center field at Double-A Birmingham, but also is expected to play the outfield some in the Arizona Fall League, while continuing to see time in the infield. Bonemer, 20, has 33 home runs this season, the most by a Sox minor leaguer in 15 years. But league scouts view him as a below-average infielder in a Sox organization full of superior defenders.</p><p><b>Nishida at the ready</b></p><p>Outfielder <b>Rikuu Nishida</b> is in Chicago and will be activated on Tuesday for another Sox player set to be placed on bereavement leave. The Japanese-born Nishida hit a symmetrical .241/.241/.241 in 12 major league games earlier this year.</p><p><b>No timeline on Teel</b></p><p>Both catcher <b>Kyle Teel</b> (left ankle sprain) and lefty reliever <b>Chris Murphy</b> (flexor strain) will begin Triple-A rehab assignments on Tuesday. Venable said Teel will both catch and DH multiple games with Charlotte, and return when the Sox “can confirm he’s performing well, he’s feeling good and he’s recovering well.”</p><p><b>No mental break for Colson</b></p><p><b>Colson Montgomery</b> has been moved out of the cleanup spot and entered Monday with a .584 OPS and a 39 percent strikeout rate since the All-Star break, but Venable doesn’t see a “mental break” out of the lineup as necessary, citing a good attitude and better at-bats on the recent road trip.</p><p>“I get the question and the bigger body of work, maybe recently, but I think that right now he's in a good spot,” Venable said. “That's always on the table as a solution for guys. I just don't think that we're there yet with him, or that we're going to get there.”<br></p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Does rookie Hagen Smith's dominance out of White Sox' bullpen point to future in rotation?
entries.summary: <p>No one spins the ball quite like White Sox rookie left-hander Hagen Smith.</p><p>After pitching two perfect innings to preserve a scoreless tie with the Mets before teammate Tristan Peters’ game-winning home run Sunday, the fifth overall pick of the 2024 draft now has struck out 13 of 31 batters in eight innings since being called up to the majors Aug. 8. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/18/will-venable-pete-crow-armstrong-white-sox-cubs-hagen-smith-randal-grichuk-andrew-benintendi-analytics-kyle-teel-crosstown-classic-lenyn-sosa" target="_blank" ><u>That walk-off home run by the Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong last week?</u></a> It’s the only hit Smith has allowed against a big-leaguer.</p><p>When throwing his trademark slider, Smith doesn’t set his fingers on the seams to set his grip, instead spinning the pitch off the skin of the ball. At the tail end of his second full season in the pros, he has yet to meet someone who does it similarly.</p><p>“Kind of close, but not with no laces,” said Smith, who won’t be tweaking his method anytime soon.</p><p>Of the players picked behind him in a loaded 2024 draft class, the Pirates’ Konnor Griffin has become the consensus top prospect in baseball this spring, out-fielder Jac Caglianone has swatted 22 homers for the Royals this season and Blue Jays right-hander Trey Yesavage dominated the Dodgers in the World Series last fall.</p><p>This month has been Smith’s first opportunity to strut his stuff. Soreness in his elbow slowed him last season before a shoulder impingement knocked him out for a month this season, shifting him to a bullpen role until next spring. Around that, he has flashed wipeout stuff but has walked more than 16% of opposing hitters.</p><p>Becoming a dominant relief weapon for the Sox, who look playoff-bound, could shift his narrative quickly.</p><p>“When he’s in the zone, he’s — I don’t want to say unhittable, but it’s hard to square him up,” Sox manager Will Venable said. “We’re seeing a lot of swing-and-miss with all of his stuff in the zone. And when he’s able to do that, he’s really impactful.”</p><p>The explanation du jour for Smith’s up-turn is raising the arm slot in his delivery after it was substantially lower at the start of spring training. More consistent movement, velocity, location and arm health seem-ingly have followed.</p><p>“It was a pretty easy fix,” Smith said. “I was just getting a little scoopy for a while. Then once we fixed that, I feel like everything got helped a little bit. Slider got better, cutter got better, fastball got better. All the shapes went back to normal.”</p><p>Smith reasons that his arm angle dropped on its own while he was working on other things, such as the cutter he has developed to better keep him in the strike zone. For the Sox, the commonality is that both of Smith’s seasons in pro ball have seen him in far better form at the end that at the beginning. In the future, if they want Smith to become the rotation solution they desperately could use right now, that cycle must end.</p><p>“Coming into spring training physically where he wants to be at is definitely a focus for everybody and for him,” Brian Bannister, the Sox’ senior adviser for pitching, told the Sun-Times. “The battle is him just being physically ready to pitch on a five-day routine for six to eight months straight, along with being pitch-efficient enough to be able to get you five to seven innings before he hits his pitch count.”</p><p>Success leaves clues. Bannister said the Sox’ biomechanists have identified some hip movements in Smith’s delivery to focus on, in addition to it becoming clear where his arm slot needs to be. The Sox drafted Smith so high because they believe his stuff is so good, his short-arm action is so deceptive and he only needs to be precise to be overwhelming.</p><p>Eight innings of relief in the majors already have provided a glimpse into what Sox scouts saw in him. Relievers can become stars in October. But is the bullpen where Smith is at his best, or is it just a template for more?</p><p>“This version, no doubt, he’s a weapon,” Bannister remarked. “We’ve kind of always known that.”</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Michael Busch trying to find version of himself that could carry Cubs: ‘I don’t feel like I’ve hit a stride’
entries.summary: <p>PHOENIX – A season ago, <b>Michael Busch</b> was the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ home-run leader.</p><p>But after smacking 34 bombs in 2025, the first baseman came into Monday sixth on the roster with just 16 this year.</p><p>It’s not that he hasn’t been effective – his .352 on-base percentage was the highest of his young major league career – but he hasn’t been the same lineup-carrying presence he was at times last season.</p><p>The Cubs’ offense has been plenty productive without Busch’s pop, waking up Monday as baseball’s highest-scoring team.</p><p>But Busch could still be that guy, and though center fielder <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/02/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-player-of-the-month-june-stats-babe-ruth-lou-gehrig-shohei-ohtani" >has been arguably baseball’s best player</a> and third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b> is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/21/cubs-alex-bregman-playoffs-stats-world-series-dansby-swanson-carson-kelly-craig-counsell" >having a tremendous second half</a>, that would be a big thing for a Cubs team seeking a deep October run.</p><p>“Michael had an incredible offensive season last year,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Sunday. “When you do that as a really young player, we all want to go, ‘Oh, that’s how it’s going to be, and it’s going to even get better.’</p><p>“But he has not hit for the power you would have expected after a season like last year, and that may be just that he didn’t get in that mode this year and he didn’t hit them in bunches like we’ve seen him hit them in the past.</p><p>“He’s still got a six-week stretch where he can do that, and that still could come.”</p><p>Busch pointed to a slow start as something of a defining moment for his season so far.</p><p>He hit just .224 with only four home runs and a .361 slugging percentage in his first 51 games. He came into Monday batting .256 with 12 homers and a .416 slugging percentage in the 78 games since.</p><p>But Busch is still waiting for that other version of himself to arrive, the guy who could be the difference as the lights get their brightest.</p><p>“I feel like I’m not tapping into what I’m capable of, in a sense,” he said Monday. “The stretch at the beginning [of the season], trying to find a groove, find a rhythm, that took me a little longer than I would have hoped. But just grinding through that, I learned a lot about me as a player, my swing, what makes me click.</p><p>“Battling some of those things has helped me going forward, though I don’t feel like I’ve hit a stride. So it’s still continuing to work and trying to find that stride. I’m playing all right, but I haven’t hit that stride that you look for – but [a stride] you also don’t try to press upon, because you understand the game.</p><p>“I’m just trying to work, continue to grind and do what I can to help this team win the rest of the year.”</p><p><b>Brown working back</b></p><p>Should one more round of live batting practice go well for righty pitcher <b>Ben Brown</b>, he could soon begin a minor league rehab assignment, the notable next step as he works back from a stress fracture in a vertebra in his neck that knocked him out in late June.</p><p>Though Brown excelled as a starter earlier this season, posting a 1.70 ERA in eight starts, he is expected to return in a relief role, a potentially intriguing weapon as the Cubs head toward the postseason.</p><p><b>Shaw update</b></p><p>Utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b> is on a minor league rehab assignment with Triple-A Iowa, with four hits in his first three games.</p><p>“We got some good health feedback from the first three days,” Counsell said, “now we’ve got to get some at-bats under his belt.”</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: How Cubs’ starters-turned-relievers allow Craig Counsell to make playoff-style pitching decisions in August
entries.summary: <p>PHOENIX — You might have heard that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> are in a playoff race.</p><p>While there’s still more than a month of baseball before the postseason begins and the Cubs play their most important games of the year, the games are pretty important already, with the Brewers threatening to pull away in the NL Central and teams like the Phillies and Padres hot on the Cubs’ heels in the wild-card standings.</p><p>And though the Cubs adhere to pro sports’ favorite strategy of taking things one game at a time — going as far as citing it as a key element of their success — they’re still playing like a team with expectations of a deep October run as the stakes increase down the stretch.</p><p>Just look at Sunday’s victory against the Mariners. Though it ended up being a 19-2 laugher, things were close early. With lefty starter Shota Imanaga struggling and the Cubs fresh off taking the lead in the top of the third inning on Ian Happ’s grand slam, manager Craig Counsell didn’t wait around to see if the southpaw could figure things out. The skipper brought out the quick hook, and Imanaga was done after recording only six outs, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/23/cubs-mariners-brewers-nl-central-standings-shota-imanaga-stats-starting-rotation-playoffs" >the shortest start of his major-league career</a>.</p><p>Considering the only thing the Cubs can do to make up ground on the Brewers when they’re not playing their division rivals is to win the game in front of them, this aggressive move made sense, the Cubs needing a win after losing the first two games of the weekend series in walk-off fashion.</p><p>But Counsell wouldn’t have made that playoff-style move — starters typically have much shorter leashes in the very different world of postseason pitching — without his contingent of long relievers in his bullpen.</p><p>“This is why we have some length in the bullpen. We can do things like this with the length in the bullpen,” Counsell said after the game. “As soon as Ian hit the home run, honestly, my thought was, ‘If Shota’s in trouble, we’re going to go. We have length. We have innings to cover if the game goes wrong. We’ve got Colin [Rea] or Aaron [Civale] to cruise through the game.’</p><p>“It was the time to do it, and that’s why we’ve got those guys down there.”</p><p>The Cubs maybe didn’t draw things up this way, but they’ve wound up with numerous would-be starters in their relief corps after Jed Hoyer’s front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >brought in a couple top-of-the-rotation arms at the trade deadline</a>.</p><p>Guys like Rea and Javier Assad – the latter stashed in the minors as the Cubs play by baseball’s roster rules – are relief options in situations like Sunday’s, able to log the innings that would have been expected of starters like Imanaga and prevent Counsell from having to wreck his bullpen by using a bevy of arms to get through the game.</p><p>Civale was the savior Sunday, throwing four scoreless innings of one-hit ball in Imanaga’s wake to preserve the ‘pen.</p><p>On a day when his lineup produced 19 runs and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/23/cubs-grand-slams-same-game-ian-happ-pedro-ramirez-mariners-home-runs-aaron-civale-shota-imanaga-craig-counsell-little-league-classic-2027" >two of his players hit grand slams</a>, Counsell said Civale’s work was “the story of the game” for him, bringing to mind the manager’s description of Assad’s 6 1/3 innings of scoreless relief in a June game as “heroic.”</p><p>Counsell could have a bullpen full of those types of pitchers come October. In addition to Rea and Assad — and possibly Civale, who was part of the Cubs’ playoff roster last year, pitching 4 1/3 scoreless innings in Game 1 of the NLDS — right-handers Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown are expected to return from their respective injuries as relievers.</p><p>It’s only a luxury if those guys keep pitching well. But they have to this point, giving Counsell the option of pulling out quick hooks and plotting playoff-style pitching decisions well before the postseason arrives.</p><p>Because hey, these games are important, too.</p><p>“There’s a lot of confidence being instilled,” said Civale, whose work Sunday moved his ERA in a Cubs uniform this season down to 1.80 in 20 innings. “It’s just taking the ball whenever you’re called upon and going out there and getting outs.”</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Enes Kanter Freedom brought middle-school energy to the WNBA
entries.summary: <p>Can men handle the mainstream success of the WNBA?</p><p>The middle-school energy they’re bringing to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> games lately has me wondering.</p><p>I thought about that during the game Friday against the Valkyries when a barrage of sex toys landed on the court.</p><p>I thought about it again Sunday, when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/23/skys-playoff-hopes-officially-end-in-tense-loss-to-fever" target="_blank" >Enes Kanter Freedom showed up to the game against the Fever</a>. The former NBA player recently mocked the league and the queer community by claiming to be a woman and declaring for the 2027 WNBA Draft.</p><p>By Monday, the league reportedly had declared him ineligible. But Sunday, he was still playing the part of a WNBA prospect.</p><p>At halftime, I found him posing for pictures next to the women’s bathroom. As I stared up at all 6 feet, 10 inches of him, I thought: Is there anything more gay than going to a women’s basketball game and having your handler photograph you next to the women’s bathroom?</p><p>It wasn’t an original thought. That was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/21/skys-natasha-cloud-calls-out-offenders-after-sex-toys-thrown-onto-court" target="_blank" >Natasha Cloud’s message</a> to the dildo-throwers Friday: Bringing a sex toy to a women’s basketball game was about the gayest thing they could do. Stop attacking marginalized groups, she told them, and admit you’re one of us.</p><p>Even though I thought it was genuinely funny, hearing her call the offenders gay made me tense.</p><p>Suddenly, I was back in middle school, calling people gay as an insult, even though deep down I knew it was cruel, even though deep down I knew I was one of them.</p><p>Cloud’s joke, I think, was exposing that exact dynamic: We hide to protect ourselves from other people, only for the hiding to hurt us even more.</p><p>Still, I remembered how easy it was to adopt their logic.</p><p>I sensed that insulting Kanter Freedom or making him the butt of a joke would cut me off from the reality of the situation.</p><p>Who is Enes, and what is he doing here?</p><p>Who am I, and what am I doing here?</p><p>Those felt like necessary questions. But it was halftime, and although I had made good progress on my game story, this was Sky-Fever in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/09/the-wnbas-gratitude-police-have-a-blind-spot-for-fevers-sophie-cunningham" target="_blank" >Sophie Cunningham’s WNBA</a>. You have to stay ready for anything.</p><p>So I walked behind Kanter Freedom back to my seat and wished for simplicity. I wanted him to disappear into the crowd, so I wouldn’t have to give him another thought.</p><p>That didn’t happen.</p><p>Cloud hit a huge layup, then turned, screamed and pointed at Kanter Freedom in his courtside seat. He stepped forward and spread his arms wide.</p><p>He was doing what he had come to do: Make himself a martyr for “protecting women’s sports.” Give talking heads another chance to call the WNBA messy, unserious and unworthy.</p><p>After the game, Sky coach Tyler Marsh made his familiar plea for people to focus on the good in the league, on the players playing. Then he addressed Kanter Freedom directly.</p><p>“If you come to a game, you should probably come to enjoy the basketball,” Marsh said. “It seems pretty simple to me.”</p><p>A few days earlier, Marsh and I had talked about why he left the NBA coaching ranks for the WNBA, even after “a hundred people” told him not to.</p><p>He found more purpose here, he said, in a league with a shared sense of fighting for something. He wished the fight weren’t necessary. But it was, and it created a sense of belonging.</p><p>Something clicked.</p><p>No wonder queer players such as Sydney Colson and Theresa Plaisance call him their favorite person. No wonder Cloud respects Marsh so much, often praising his steadiness and emotional control.</p><p>“When you talk about men, we love when they can regulate their emotions,” she had told the Sun-Times earlier that week.</p><p>Maybe because of Cloud, Marsh or Kanter Freedom, I spent the next day with this question:</p><p>What is a good man?</p><p>Is it a coach such as Marsh, drawn to the league by its collective struggle? Is it an NBA player such as Kevin Durant, who invests in relationships with young WNBA stars?</p><p>Maybe. Still, it didn’t seem that simple.</p><p>And then, because I was no longer writing a game story, because I finally had a moment to be queer and expansive and make room for complexity:</p><p>What is a man, anyway?</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Armed robbers fatally shoot man, 36, during heist at Brighton Park gas station
entries.summary: <p>Armed robbers fatally shot a man at a gas station after robbing it early Tuesday on the Southwest Side. </p><p>Around 2:50 a.m., at least one gunman entered the Thorntons, 3450 S. California Ave, and took money, Chicago police said. </p><p>While fleeing with cash, one of the robbers opened fire, fatally striking a 36-year-old man multiple times in the body, police said. </p><p>The man, 36, was pronounced dead at the scene, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. His name was not released. </p><p>No arrests were made. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Working-class men need to come together as they did back in 1879
entries.summary: <p>I understood the depth of it first at a friend's 21st birthday party in college. Somebody raised a glass to celebrate him. Then another raised his and, before it reached his shoulder, tipped it.</p><p>He poured libations for the ones who did not make it. Shot, or sent away, before the rest of us got to college. In a room of nothing but young Black and Latino men, we all joined in.</p><p>A Latino friend from childhood, hiding from his own gang the last time I saw him. My best friend, Black, locked up for taking sunglasses from a Goodwill. A Filipino buddy shot dead that summer over a drug deal, folks said.</p><p>Splash. Splash. Splash.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a10000" name="module-a10000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Then a friend lifted his glass and toasted the plain fact that one more of us had lived to 21.</p><p>That cut me like a knife. In the richest country on Earth we were congratulating a Black man for breathing past his birthday.</p><p>That grief runs deep in our community. But it floats on deeper American water.</p><p>Not long after, my mind raced through every young man I knew who was suffering or gone. Among them, White friends whose father killed himself when we were teenagers, after the plant let him go.</p><p>Last week I promised you numbers on the crisis facing our nation's men. Here are a few.</p><p>Start with work. About 7 million American men between 25 and 54 are neither working nor looking for a job. More than one in 10. Every recovery of the last 50 years has left that share higher.</p><p>Then violence, which wears two extreme faces. In 2023 Black men were murdered, usually by other Black men, at roughly eight times the rate of white men. Meanwhile white men killed themselves at nearly twice the rate of Black men.</p><p>Then prison. America locks up more of its people than almost any nation on earth. Here is what nobody says. Count white Americans alone and they are still locked up at several times the rate of Canada, Germany or Japan.</p><p>This is a national problem, far bigger than any one community.</p><p>And yet we stay a house divided. Divide and conquer is the oldest game in America. The British brought it here to keep the king rich. The Revolution should have killed it. It did not, because it works just as well at helping the rich get richer.</p><p>Whenever working people have reason to stand together, somebody pits them against each other. Dr. King named it in Montgomery in 1965. Borrowing from historian C. Vann Woodward, he called segregation a strategy to keep the masses divided and labor cheap.</p><p>After that party I went to my grandmother's house and laid the burden on her table.</p><p>Her grandfather was Edward David Bland, born enslaved in Virginia in 1848. He was 16 when he walked out of slavery in the last days of the war, and he learned to make shoes.</p><p>Then he went into politics at the worst moment imaginable. Reconstruction was over, the troops sent home, the men who once ran the Confederacy taking it back with rifles.</p><h3>In trouble together</h3><p>He did the arithmetic anyway. Poor white farmers wanted the same free schools his people wanted. Together they were a majority. Apart they canceled each other out.</p><p>So he pushed for a deal with the unlikeliest partner in Virginia, a railroad magnate and former Confederate general named William Mahone. In 1879, Bland stood before his own people and made the case. He won them over.</p><p>They called themselves Readjusters, and they swept into power. In a few short years they abolished the whipping post, repealed the poll tax and funded schools for every child. Virginia had 415 Black teachers in 1879. Soon it had 1,588.</p><p>Then, in Danville, on Nov. 3, 1883, after a circular full of lies about Black rule swept the town, white gunmen killed at least five people, four of them Black. Three days later, white supremacists took back the legislature. The oldest trick, right on time.</p><p>Still, they had governed four years in the old capital of the Confederacy.</p><p>The men in trouble today are in trouble together. The white man in the hollowed-out mill town and the Black man on the South Side want the same thing. A better future for their children.</p><p>They are not each other's problem. Nobody is coming to tell them so.</p><p>Bland did not wait for anyone. He did the math, organized, and made it real.</p><p>The old Readjuster arithmetic still works. Divided we cancel out our children's dreams. Together our families are the majority that can make them real. Let's get to work.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-580000" name="module-580000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Bitter Ex Cut Off Dad From His Daughters
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> After nearly 18 years of marriage, I left my wife. Our daughters were 10 and 12. We had married quickly, and only later did I realize how deeply judgmental her "born-again" beliefs were — so much so that she gradually cut off my entire side of the family. I tried for years to reason with her, to no avail, and we divorced. What I never anticipated was losing my children as well.</p><p>In the years that followed, I sent cards, letters and messages — most went unanswered. I was told, "The girls don't want to see you," yet I was never given the chance to hear that directly from them. Over time, I came to realize I was a victim of parental alienation — something I never would have imagined from someone who professed strong Christian values.</p><p>More than 35 years have passed since I left that marriage, and I have had no meaningful contact with my daughters since. I am not without fault, and I own my mistakes, but the pain of lost years — and lost connection — remains. I write for others who may see themselves here: Please don't let years pass in silence. Talk. Listen. Apologize. Seek understanding before distance becomes permanent. — <i>MR. KALAMAZOO</i></p><p><b>DEAR MR. KALAMAZOO:</b> You have my sympathy for the years of pain and separation you've endured. Your story shows the importance of seeking partial custody or visitation rights as part of a divorce settlement. Your ex-wife would have had a much harder time cutting you off from your daughters if you'd had a court-mandated right to spend time with them. What's done is done. You must allow yourself to accept it and live your life.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am feeling uncomfortable with what has become a steady stream of requests on social media for charitable contributions on friends' birthdays. My husband and I carefully budget our annual charitable contributions, and we try to be as generous as possible, but we cannot possibly respond to all of these requests and still fund our own preferences.</p><p>Would it be rude to post a comment saying, "Although this is not one of our charitable priorities, we wish you a happy birthday!"? My best friend says it would be better not to respond at all, but that feels a bit rude. What do you think? — <i>UNHAPPY BIRTHDAYS IN MONTANA</i></p><p><b>DEAR UNHAPPY:</b> Do not state that the charity the person has chosen is low on your list of priorities. Acknowledge the occasion by posting warm wishes for the birthday to be a special one. Period.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My daughter is 19 and has a job. She has had a friend since fifth grade. They went six months without talking, but now they're friends again. My daughter offers to buy her stuff, but I feel it's not fair of the friend to accept. She works, too, but she doesn't have enough money for any activities other than lunch. I want to stay out of it, but it bothers me. What should I do? — <i>PROUD MOM IN MASSACHUSETTS</i></p><p><b>DEAR MOM:</b> Stay out of it. If the arrangement becomes so out of balance that it begins to bother your daughter, she will deal with it without your involvement. If she wants your advice, she'll ask for it.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned the column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.summary: <p>At <a class="Link" href="https://www.smythchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Smyth</u></a>, the tasting menu on any given night might include petals from Chicago-grown magnolia trees atop caramelized eel on brioche toast or quail eggs marinated with spring onions, black walnut and caviar. There’s also the pistachio praline tart with a kombu (kelp) shell and passionfruit, or the braised abalone and maitake mushrooms, with a server-drizzled sauce made from abalone stock, mushrooms, brown butter, sea lettuce and ogo.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-720000" name="image-720000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2a74a75/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7360x4131+0+391/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa4%2F84%2F928aae964e6791d3b741a9cb04f5%2F2026-05-20-smyth-monterrey-bay-abalone-6539-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cefa755/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7360x4131+0+391/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa4%2F84%2F928aae964e6791d3b741a9cb04f5%2F2026-05-20-smyth-monterrey-bay-abalone-6539-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d10651c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7360x4131+0+391/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa4%2F84%2F928aae964e6791d3b741a9cb04f5%2F2026-05-20-smyth-monterrey-bay-abalone-6539-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The Monterey Bay abalone dish, served at Smyth. The dish includes maitake mushrooms and is served with a tableside sauce made from abalone stock, mushrooms, brown butter, sea lettuce and ogo." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d10651c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7360x4131+0+391/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa4%2F84%2F928aae964e6791d3b741a9cb04f5%2F2026-05-20-smyth-monterrey-bay-abalone-6539-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/aec69e1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7360x4131+0+391/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa4%2F84%2F928aae964e6791d3b741a9cb04f5%2F2026-05-20-smyth-monterrey-bay-abalone-6539-1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d10651c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7360x4131+0+391/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa4%2F84%2F928aae964e6791d3b741a9cb04f5%2F2026-05-20-smyth-monterrey-bay-abalone-6539-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Smyth’s Monterey Bay abalone dish includes maitake mushrooms and is served with a sauce made from abalone stock, mushrooms, brown butter, sea lettuce and ogo.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided/Kevin Eduard White</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But head downstairs, and you’ll find Smyth’s more casual counterpart: <a class="Link" href="https://www.theloyalistchicago.com/" target="_blank" >The Loyalist</a>. On the menu is the “OG cheeseburger,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2026/04/01/best-burgers-chicago-list" target="_blank" ><u>often touted as one of Chicago’s best</u></a> ($28).</p><p>The patty, made of beef chuck and pork bacon, is served on a sesame seed bun with American cheese and pickled and charred onions. During happy hour (5-7 p.m. Monday through Thursday), the burger combo comes with a Miller High Life and shot of whiskey for $28.</p><p>In today’s thin-margined restaurant economy, owners John Shields and Karen Urie Shields, the husband-and-wife duo behind the establishments, have learned a critical lesson: that you can't run a high-end dining destination without a middle-of-the-road offset. Smyth can’t exist without burger-forward The Loyalist (which opened downstairs, one month before the fine-dining spot more than 10 years ago) and vice versa.</p><p>When Smyth first opened in 2016, the tasting menu <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.eater.com/2016/8/23/12608962/smyth-menu-west-loop-shields" target="_blank" ><u>cost $135</u></a> per person. A decade later, its tasting menu comes with a price tag that’s more than 200% of what it originally cost at $420 per person — all thanks to inflation, food supply chain issues, labor costs and rising prices that impact the restaurant economy.</p><p>The pair have learned they couldn’t do it alone: The success of their restaurants, much like their romantic relationship, is built on a strong foundation of friendship, creativity and teamwork.</p><p>But even after being <a class="Link" href="https://www.theworlds50best.com/" target="_blank" ><u>named No. 1 restaurant in North America</u></a> of 2026 in May by 50 Best, the Shieldses are feeling the strain of running a business. Smyth is also the only Chicago restaurant to bear three Michelin stars (<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2025/11/12/alinea-michelin-star-grant-achatz-smyth-chicago-top-restaurants-awards" target="_blank" ><u>after Alinea lost a star in November</u></a>).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-280000" name="image-280000"></a> The restaurant was awarded its third Michelin star in 2023.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Despite rising inflation, shrinking margins and the ultra-competitive culinary scene in Chicago, Smyth has ascended to global prominence. And the fine-dining establishment at 177 N. Ada St. in the West Loop is celebrating another big milestone with its 10th anniversary on Wednesday.</p><p>But even with that designation, they’re facing increasing challenges, says John, who is executive chef. Karen is Smyth’s head pastry chef. Over the past decade, they’ve settled into a partnership that allows John to handle back-of-house operations, while Karen handles pastry and more of the business side. And a decade after opening, the city and world look significantly different than they did in 2016.</p><p>“[We] can adjust prices, especially with accolades,” John said. “But we try not to gouge either... labor’s expensive, product’s expensive.”</p><p>And in a city like Chicago, The Loyalist faces plenty of competition, especially in the burger world. “We always wanted [The Loyalist] to be a neighborhood place that was really loyal to classic cooking techniques,” Karen said. “We like to be authentic.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Raising prices any higher is out of the question for now, however, as the Shieldses try to stay committed to their approach to food that elevated them to the echelon of the culinary world. </p><h3><b>From local farms to your plate</b></h3><p>At Smyth, the food is created with the farm-to-table model in mind. And to set themselves apart, the Shieldses have invested in sourcing produce that you can’t always find on your typical grocery store shelves.</p><p>Each Saturday morning, just a few people get up at the crack of dawn to get the first picks of produce from the <a class="Link" href="https://www.google.com/aclk?sa=L&pf=1&ai=DChsSEwiE8I-GwKuWAxUsgMIIHSrZCmwYACICCAEQARoCamY&co=1&ase=2&gclid=CjwKCAjwhZDUBhBGEiwAbi5bjto0J3rTTBZXF9duXo-mg-vVRuLXtTLPEpfW3LPKrTvggrFUtp6uOBoC5a0QAvD_BwE&ei=aAGFaubYM8zCruEP6te00Qc&cid=CAASWuRothr6S_OZkAIAvwQ9kd7i-wcco4MpPy69ynBQj2buxLl3uoOAYu9si-loEWfpbiUJXahyEAp7eM9KPIg323hEjFuw3NdUsKwgjsMoHCNNfqgc_QqDgoe4aQ&cce=2&category=acrcp_v1_32&sig=AOD64_0GCL9A-Z56nsMLDKebhrsvt3fxrw&q&sqi=2&nis=4&adurl=https://www.greencitymarket.org?gad_source%3D1%26gad_campaignid%3D15856557264%26gbraid%3D0AAAAADNIfRiinoPnFoMVT1fyRYiQHAhB-%26gclid%3DCjwKCAjwhZDUBhBGEiwAbi5bjto0J3rTTBZXF9duXo-mg-vVRuLXtTLPEpfW3LPKrTvggrFUtp6uOBoC5a0QAvD_BwE&ved=2ahUKEwjmrIiGwKuWAxVMoSsGHeorLXoQ0Qx6BAgWEAE" target="_blank" ><u>Green City Market</u></a> in Lincoln Park. </div><p>“John is there in his chef’s whites, lugging produce from farms to his car on his way into work at 6:30 in the morning,” said Jason Hammel, owner and executive chef at Lula Cafe in Logan Square, in a recent chat. “And clearly, his day is not going to end for very many hours.”</p><p>One example of the unique and rare produce they’ve brought into Smyth is kakai, a small squash variety with light flesh. They were grown by Jerry Boone of <a class="Link" href="https://www.greencitymarket.org/farmer/details/boone-beloit" target="_blank" ><u>Froggy Meadow Farm</u></a> in Beloit, Wisconsin, who has also been working on a Japanese yam for the restaurant for about two years.</p><p>John said the kakai will be served in some fall dishes. Growing specialty produce is no small task and isn’t necessarily cheap, which adds to Smyth’s operating costs (he said that eggs from a particular farmer cost $45 per dozen). But working with farmers in and out of the Midwest is an investment, John says. entries.title: O'Hare to the Loop in 15 minutes? This company thinks it can finally bring fast rail to Chicago
entries.summary: <p></p><p>People have tried and failed over the years to build a nonstop, quick rail connection from the Loop to O'Hare International Airport. Think of Elon Musk's proposed crosstown tunnel from the unfinished superstation in the basement of Block 37.</p><p>But a new company says they can succeed where others have failed.</p><p>They call it the O’Hare Flyer.</p><p>They envision a 15-minute trip from the Old Post Office to O’Hare on battery-powered trains leaving every 15 minutes at an average of 80 mph — and with tickets much cheaper than a ride-share.</p><p>The $2.25 billion pitch is from veteran Chicago train consultant Mark Walbrun — who led the redesign of Chicago Union Station in the 1990s — and fellow cofounders David Lundy, a strategic consultant, and Kristi Lafleur, former director of the Illinois Tollway and former CEO of the Chicago Skyway.</p><p>"Everyone who's tried to do this is replicating the Blue Line ... or a tunnel like Musk. ... None of that works," says Lundy, O’Hare Flyer’s CEO.</p><p>The key to success, they say, is using newly freed up freight railroad land at a Union Pacific yard on the Near West Side.</p><p>It's now possible for a private company to run quick crosstown service — through the West and Northwest sides — with minimal construction on 100% dedicated tracks, they say.</p><p>"This is the only way we can make this happen," Lundy says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9f0000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A rendering of the proposed O’Hare Flyer’s station at Terminal 2.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>O’Hare Flyer</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>They plan to build a station just west of the Old Post Office, using the long abandoned tracks under Canal Street. Heading to O'Hare, trains would initially go south and turn west near Roosevelt Road, where they'd navigate a mix of CSX and UP rail lines before turning north on Canadian National tracks, which would be expanded with an additional dedicated track.</p><p>Trains will run along a single track, except for 6 miles of double track midway along the route so trains can pass each other, Lundy says.</p><p>At O'Hare, the company plans to build a 90-foot track flyover above the two-plane taxiways that cross over I-190. Tracks will have to be built along the ring road, with a platform covering the length of Terminal 2, with easy connections to Terminals 1 and 3, and a short distance from the "people mover" connection to Terminal 5.</p><p>O'Hare Flyer has a tentative agreement with freight company CSX, and "a pathway to 'Yes'" with CN and UP, Lundy says. Their team also has briefed Mayor Brandon Johnson, whose aviation and transportation departments must approve the construction of tracks near the Old Post office and O'Hare.</p><p>Johnson, in a statement, said the proposal "is just the latest evidence of the growing confidence private investors" have in the city, and that his "administration looks forward to further discussions with those seeking to make transformative investments in Chicago."</p><p>The project could be finished in five years, Lundy says, and preliminary construction could begin in 2027.</p><p>The trains could be similar to the battery-powered ones recently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/02/21/metra-battery-train-zero-emission-stadler" target="_blank" >ordered by Metra</a>, made either by Stadler or Siemens Mobility. Those trains have a top speed of 120 mph and can go 60 miles on a single charge, well beyond the 20 miles between O'Hare and downtown.</p><p>The fare for each trip hasn't been set, but will be more than the Blue Line but less than an Uber, Lyft or other ride-hailing service, which typically costs over $50.</p><p>Four trains would operate simultaneously and run daily from 4 a.m. to 10 p.m.</p><p>As for the $2.25 billion price tag, the group says this will be a mainly commercially funded venture. They won't say how much they've raised, but say fundraising shouldn't be a problem once they get the final OKs from the city and rail companies.</p><p>Any construction timeline depends on those final approvals and the community engagement process, which could begin soon after the downtown station design in the next few months.</p><p>The project could be a major win for Chicago, if completed, says Joseph Schwieterman, director of DePaul University's Chaddick Institute for Metropolitan Development.</p><p>"A remarkable set of opportunities have opened up to make this possible," he said, citing the available freight tracks and private financing. And battery-powered train technology is finally feasible, he says, "that's much more affordable than some of the pie-in-the-sky proposals of the past."</p><p>In 2018, Musk was chosen by then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/6/13/18478521/elon-musk-chosen-to-build-operate-o-hare-express-dubbed-tesla-in-a-tunnel" target="_blank" >to build an underground tunnel</a> from downtown to O'Hare, with then-untested "Hyperloop" technology that promised 12-minute trips, $25 each, in autonomous vehicles racing over 100 mph. The project fell through after Emanuel chose not to seek reelection and Musk was scrutinized for smoking pot on Joe Rogan's podcast.</p><p>Schwieterman said there are several risks around the O'Hare Flyer: its reliance on debt financing, the need for strong ridership to pay the bills, the potential for construction cost overruns and the reliance on a single track for most of its service.</p><p>Chicago's business community has long wanted a quick, direct rail link between downtown and O'Hare, Lundy says. A trip on the CTA Blue Line train can take over an hour, sometimes, between downtown and the airport.</p><p>Phil Clement, president and CEO of World Business Chicago, says he has been working with the O'Hare Flyer team for over a year. "If realized, this investment will strengthen [Chicago's] competitive position across business and tourism," he said in a statement.</p><p>Walbrun has been thinking of an O'Hare rail link for two decades. Dozens of major cities worldwide have them — but Chicago doesn't.</p><p>"If we're a world-class city," Lundy says, "let's have a world class transportation system."</p>

entries.title: Bears unveil new alternate uniform — and it has orange pants
entries.summary: <p>The Bears unveiled an alternate uniform Tuesday — and it has an orange helmet. And orange pants.</p><p>In between the two is a navy jersey with orange numbers outlined in white.</p><p>The number font is different than the style of the Bears' standard uniforms; rather, it's similar to their 1948 uniforms. The stripes on the sleeves run vertical, not horizontal, and harken back to the vertical stripes across the front of the jersey of some of the Bears' earliest teams. The orange helmet is the same one they released in 2022, though with a new "Bears" nose bumper and Chicago stars stripped across the back padding.</p><p>With George S. Halas' initials removed from the sleeve, the Bears will wear a "GHS" patch in the shape of a football on their chest. It's the same patch they wore after his death in 1983 and similar to the Virginia McCaskey memorial patch they wore last year.</p><p>The look resembles the University of Illinois — but then again, it always has. The Bears wear navy and orange because those were the colors of Halas' alma mater.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> will wear the uniform just once this year: on Christmas Day against the Packers. The Packers will wear theirs in Week 5 against the Bears. Teams can keep the "Rivalries" uniform in their rotation for up to three years.</p><p>The Bears' standard uniforms will remain the same.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Monsters never die. They are reborn. <a href="https://t.co/E7D2oGqi8t">pic.twitter.com/E7D2oGqi8t</a></p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2092250690026668499?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The team also released a retro-inspired logo — an orange football with the word Chicago written across it and a navy bear crawling over it.</p><p>Nike began the "Rivalries" program a year ago, unveiling alternate uniforms for teams from the AFC East and the NFC West. This year, the company, which has exclusive rights to produce NFL on-field uniforms and apparel, worked with teams from the NFC North and AFC South to develop their alternates. The Bears designed those uniforms without wanting to compromise their brand, which is as consistent and traditional as any team in NFL history. But for a few details, the Bears' standard home and away uniforms have remained the same since 1963, when they first put decals on their helmets.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Every stitch tells a story 🧵 <a href="https://t.co/JUH1jDFPFi">pic.twitter.com/JUH1jDFPFi</a></p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2092258227689828542?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Bears chairman George McCaskey, who has a keen interest in the team's past and present uniforms, has always been a traditionalist. When his mother Virginia died last year, he honored her not only <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/07/30/bears-virginia-mccaskey-tribute-patch-george-no-throwbacks-alternate-uniforms-steve-mcmichael" target="_blank" >with a jersey patch</a> but by having the team wear their traditional home and away uniforms all year long, the way she liked it. The team briefly shelved its orange and striped uniform sets. When the Bears hosted two playoff games, McCaskey decided to pair the Bears' traditional home navy jerseys with their road navy pants.</p><p>All eight "Rivalries" teams unveiled their uniforms online at the same time Tuesday morning. The Bears will address theirs further following Tuesday afternoon's practice at Halas Hall.</p>

entries.title: Thousands in Northwest Indiana still don't have power after storms. Here's what to know.
entries.summary: <p>Northwest Indiana residents continue suffering after back-to-back storms devastated the state earlier this month. </p><p>Winds of nearly 100 mph and torrential downpours knocked trees into people's homes and driveways and flooded basements and roads. Seven people died across Indiana. The storms caused widespread power outages in much of the state. </p><p>While power has been restored for over 300,000 Hoosiers, many residents are still without power. Gary, one of Indiana's hardest-hit cities, had the most customers in the state waiting for power to return, according to the NIPSCO, Northwest Indiana's electric utility company.</p><p>As of Tuesday morning, 97% of NIPSCO customers who had lost power had their service restored. In Gary, about 2,000 customers remained without power.</p><p>Here's what to know about what happened in Northwest Indiana and the relief efforts underway. </p><h3>When will Northwest Indiana cities get their power back? </h3><p>NIPSCO reported that more than 60% of its customers — roughly 370,000 — lost power during the Aug. 11 storm and subsequent days of severe weather. </p><p> Gary and Portage residents are expected to have to wait till Tuesday for their power to return — two weeks after the Aug. 11 storm. <a class="Link" href="https://www.nipsco.com/outages/power-outages" target="_blank" >Here’s the full list</a> of towns still waiting on power.</p><h3>Why is it taking so long? </h3><p>Part of why it’s taking longer to restore power is the city suffered the most “extensive and complex damage” from the storm, mainly because of the 99 mph winds that tore through Northwest Indiana and knocked down several large trees, a NIPSCO executive has said.</p><div class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A week after the storms, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/17/gary-indiana-residents-without-power-deadly-storms" target="_blank" >residents showed the Sun-Times</a> the extent of the damage. The worst was caused by mature large trees falling on their properties.</p><p>Crews of linemen are repairing downed power lines and rebuilding destroyed electrical systems. That includes 335 damaged poles that need to be repaired or replaced and 27 outages at substations that need to be fixed before power can be restored.</p><h3>Why did ComEd restore power faster for the south suburbs?</h3><p>The same storm system that hit Indiana also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/seven-7-confirmed-tornadoes-weather-service-illinois-monday-storms" target="_blank" >caused seven tornadoes</a> in Chicago's south suburbs. Soon after the storm, ComEd was able to restore power for the vast majority of its customers.</p><p>Melody Birmingham, the group utilities president at NiSource, NIPSCO’s parent company, tried to explain Wednesday why it's taken the utility longer to restore power compared to ComEd. ComEd has 4 million customers, compared to NIPSCO's 500,000. That means the utility has a much larger staff and is better equipped to respond to outages faster.</p><h3>Are schools still closed? </h3><p>The damage caused by the storms caused many school districts to close schools until power is restored and debris is cleared.</p><p>Gary's schools have been closed all week. As of Thursday, <a class="Link" href="https://www.garycsc.k12.in.us/" target="_blank" >Gary Community School Corporation</a> was still waiting for power to return to all of the city's schools. The school district, which is posting <a class="Link" href="https://www.garycsc.k12.in.us/" target="_blank" >regular updates on its website</a>, has not said whether schools will reopen next week. </p><p>In a note posted to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.hobart.k12.in.us/" target="_blank" >School City of Hobart’s website</a>, Supt. Peggy Buffington said she anticipates schools opening Monday. </p><h3>How have businesses been affected? </h3><p>Many restaurants, gas stations, grocery stores, banks and small businesses across Northwest Indiana were also still without power. Many businesses remain closed, while others are able to partially operate. </p><p>Gary Chamber of Commerce President Charles Hughes said he does not have a timeline for when businesses will have power restored because NIPSCO is prioritizing hospitals and homes.</p><h3>What resources are available? </h3><p>Crews from FEMA and the Indiana Department of Homeland Security are assessing the damage across the state.</p><p>Indiana Gov. Mike Braun has activated <a class="Link" href="https://www.in.gov/dhs/emergency-management-and-preparedness/august-2026-disaster" target="_blank" >the state’s disaster relief fund</a>. People can <a class="Link" href="https://app.smartsheet.com/b/form/01a019f5a4457f0495bbef680cff9c75" target="_blank" >apply online for relief funds</a>. Immediate emergency grants are capped at $5,000. </p><p>Several community groups are also providing resources and shelter. The YWCA, 150 W. 15th Ave., is offering round-the-clock shelter, warm meals and charging stations. The Monroe Center, 4101 Washington St., is offering emergency shelter to residents whose homes were affected. Family Life Community Center, 565 Massachusetts St., is distributing hot meals and groceries.</p><p>Capital B Gary has compiled this <a class="Link" href="https://gary.capitalbnews.org/northwest-indiana-storm-relief-resources/" target="_blank" >list of resources</a> for those in need of help, including where to get hot meals, power for their devices and emergency shelter.</p>

</figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydoae-l-o/" target="_blank" >This company thinks it can finally bring fast rail to Chicago</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydoae-l-b/" target="_blank" >David Struett</a></h5><p><b>O'Hare Flyer</b>: People have tried and failed over the years to build a nonstop, quick rail connection from the Loop to O'Hare Airport, but a new company says it can succeed with the O'Hare Flyer — an affordable 15-minute trip from the Old Post Office to O'Hare on battery-powered trains at an average of 80 mph.</p><p><b>Who's behind this?</b>: The $2.25 billion pitch is from veteran Chicago train consultant Mark Walbrun — who led the redesign of Union Station in the 1990s — and fellow cofounders David Lundy, a strategic consultant, and Kristi Lafleur, former director of the Illinois Tollway and former CEO of the Chicago Skyway.</p><p><b>How would it work?</b>: The key to success, they say, is using newly freed-up freight railroad land at a Union Pacific yard on the Near West Side. It's now possible for a private company to run quick crosstown service — through the West and Northwest sides — with minimal construction on 100% dedicated tracks, they say. They plan to build a station just west of the Old Post Office, using the long-abandoned tracks under Canal Street.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: In 2018, Elon Musk was chosen by then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydoae-l-n/" target="_blank" >to build an underground tunnel</a> from downtown to O’Hare, with then-untested "Hyperloop" technology that promised 12-minute trips in autonomous vehicles racing over 100 mph. href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydoae-l-m/" target="_blank" >School is back in session for CPS students after summer of budget angst</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydoae-l-c/" target="_blank" >Emmanuel Camarillo</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydoae-l-q/" target="_blank" >Sarah Karp</a></h5><p><b>First day finances</b>: Chicago Public Schools classes resumed Monday for some 300,000 students, following a summer in which layoffs and last-minute budget changes made it challenging for schools to plan. CPS is now in the process of rehiring laid-off staff and placing them at schools with vacancies while officials wait to see if the state or city will come through with the extra revenue that CPS is counting on.</p><p><b>The positives</b>: District officials point to the addition of special education staff to support the rising number of CPS students with disabilities, and the expansion of dual language and world language programs that help students learn a language other than English.</p><p><b>Around the city</b>: With a DJ playing hip-hop and balloons flying overhead, students were welcomed back to Leland Elementary, where Mayor Brandon Johnson rang the ceremonial bell. At Prosser Career Academy, fresh haircuts and first-day selfies defined the day. And for Burnetta Cox, Monday marked her first day as a teacher at Revere Elementary School: "I want them to see me as someone they can depend on," she said of her new students.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydoae-l-e/" target="_blank" >Erica Thompson</a></h5><p><b>Waiting on the city</b>: Since 2020, Austin residents have been waiting for the city to build a gateway arch at the entrance of its Soul City Corridor, the stretch of Chicago Avenue from Austin Boulevard to Cicero Avenue touting several Black-owned businesses, including the Avenue Que and Kitchen, Spill the Beans coffee shop, T&C Fitness Club and Forty Acres Fresh Market.</p><p><b>High hopes:</b> Neighbors were thrilled when an artist, Bernard Williams, was selected, and renderings were drawn up. And last year, Illinois designated a larger segment of Austin as Soul City, one of 15 official cultural districts in the state, paving the way for $200,000 in additional monies to boost the neighborhood.</p><p><b>Stalled promise</b>: Gateway construction has stalled, leaving the burgeoning development of Black business, arts and culture unidentifiable to those driving from the west suburbs into the city. The delay of a single symbol illustrates how bureaucratic the process to create a cultural district in Illinois can be.</p><p><b>See for yourself</b>: From a renovated concert auditorium to a youth entries.title: Voting is being wrecked. Voting is being wrecked. Voting is...
entries.summary: <p>I try not to repeat myself.</p><p>Let me say that again.</p><p>I try not to repeat myself.</p><p>Why? Well, for starters, it becomes dull. The second time never carries the punch of the first. You've read it before, maybe. The impact lessens.</p><p>Even if I try to switch things around.</p><p>Repeating myself is something I try not to do.</p><p>But what if the same thing keeps happening? Something important. And any other topic, well, pales in comparison.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c70000" name="module-c70000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/08/24/supreme-court-trump-administration-mail-voting-restrictions-ruling-midterms" >On Monday, the United States Supreme Court </a>said to President Donald Trump, in essence: "Sure, go ahead and mess with the mail-in ballots, part of your general campaign to undermine and muddy elections, in case your side loses and you have to toss over the game board and cry 'Unfair!' your go-to move for years and years."</p><p>In October, 2016, when it looked liked the tide might be turning for Hillary Clinton, Trump fired off a series of tweets.</p><p>"Of course there is large scale voter fraud happening on and before election day."</p><p>And...</p><p>"The election is absolutely being rigged by the dishonest and distorted media pushing Crooked Hillary — but also at many polling places — SAD."</p><p>And... speaking of repetition.</p><p>"Election is being rigged by the media, in a coordinated effort with the Clinton campaign..."</p><p>Then he won, and... poof... suddenly the election was fine. Though Republican candidates, in parroting Trump's claims, would insist that elections that they themselves won were also rigged. Which would be funny. If the situation weren't so terrifying. </p><p>In the 2020 election, which Trump clearly and definitively lost to Joe Biden, the only dramatic attempts at election fraud were the president's, demanding that Georgia election officials "find" votes to put him over the top. Since then, he has machine-gunned lies about the election.</p><p>Not to forget the Jan. 6, 2021 insurrection. After which the nation re-elected him anyway, which tempts a person to give up, sit back, and declare we deserve whatever we get. </p><p>Maybe we do.</p><p>In 2024, Trump beat the drum constantly. He claimed the election was being rigged. Hundreds of times.</p><p>Which leads to now, and me wanting to stand on a chair, bang two garbage can lids together, and scream something I've been saying for quite a long time. Most recently in March, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/03/12/midterm-primary-election-illinois-importance-of-voting" target="_blank" >in a column</a> about voting in the primary. This is the very last paragraph, which I can reprint because, attention spans being what they are, I know that many readers never get to the last paragraph, not with Instagram and TikTok right there, demanding attention:</p><p>"To me, election integrity is the most important issue facing us. If we can’t vote, we can’t influence government, and it can do whatever it likes, unchecked. We see that in action now. One way to understand our current administration is this: They’re acting like they will never leave power. Whether they are correct or not depends on the survival of free and fair elections."</p><p>Elsewhere in the column, I quote the Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan law and policy organization, which offered up its “<a class="Link" href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/timeline-trump-administrations-efforts-undermine-elections" target="_blank" >Timeline of the Trump Administration’s Efforts to Undermine Elections.”</a></p><p>It lays out, in painful detail, using color-coding to help make various strategies clear, "a concerted strategy to undermine U.S. elections."</p><p>Heck, its opening bears repeating as well:</p><p>“In 2025, a new threat to free and fair elections emerged: the federal government.</p><p>“Since day one of his second term, the Trump administration has attempted to rewrite election rules to burden voters and usurp control of election systems, targeted and threatened election officials and others who keep elections free and fair, supported people who undermine election administration, and retreated from the federal government’s role of protecting voters and the electoral process.”</p><p>Pause a moment to consider why Trump says he's doing this. To prevent voter fraud, specifically by non-citizens. Which scarcely exists. Allow me to quote the Bipartisan Policy Center: "Illegal voting, including by noncitizens, is routinely investigated and prosecuted by the appropriate authorities, and there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome. When investigating noncitizen voting, it is important to distinguish between voter registration and casting a ballot. Noncitizen registration is already rare, and noncitizen voting is even less common."</p><p>This must be said again and again, in part, because Democrats don't seem to get it. You would think that keeping America a representative democracy would provide a compelling platform for Democrats to run on. But apparently they see this as the moment to focus on side issues. Other policy questions are important, true. But if the voting process is destroyed, nothing else matters.</p><p>If the voting process is destroyed, nothing else matters.</p><p>If the voting process is destroyed...</p>

entries.title: Armored truck robbed at Roseland Burger King
entries.summary: <p>Police are on the scene where several masked armed gunmen robbed an armored truck at a Roseland neighborhood Burger King at midday. </p><p>It happened at the Burger King, 110 E. 95th St., according to police. </p><p>Three armed masked men, who were armed with guns at a rifle, robbed a Loomis armored truck before fleeing in a car, possibly heading to the expressway, dispatchers relayed over police radio. </p><p>Further details were not immediately available. </p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p>
