entries.title: Chicago History Museum workers ratify first union contract
entries.summary: <p>Workers at the Chicago History Museum have ratified their first union contract, after what the union representing the workers called “some of the worst anti-union retaliation we’ve seen.”</p><p>In May, the National Labor Relations Board issued <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2026/05/18/chicago-history-museum-labor-law-firing-employees-unionizing-nlrb" target="_blank" ><u>a rare formal complaint</u></a>, alleging that under the museum’s previous president, Donald Lassere, management retaliated against employees who <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/museums/2025/02/12/chicago-history-museum-unionize-employees-union-afscme" target="_blank" ><u>voted to unionize in 2025</u></a>.</p><p>Shortly after that vote, four employees were fired, while others were disciplined or threatened with termination, according to the NLRB. The board found the museum <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/work/2026/05/18/chicago-history-museum-labor-law-firing-employees-unionizing-nlrb" target="_blank" ><u>violated federal labor laws</u></a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/01/07/chicago-history-museum-president-out-donald-e-lassere" target="_blank" ><u>Lassere exited the role in January</u></a> after nearly five years at the helm. Last month, the museum named Michael J. Anderson as Lassere’s successor to lead the Lincoln Park museum. In July, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/museums/2026/07/30/chicago-history-museum-names-new-president-ceo-michael-anderson-lincoln-park" target="_blank" ><u>Anderson told WBEZ</u></a> the museum extended offers to the four ousted employees to return to work at the museum as part of settling the NLRB complaint, saying management was committed to negotiating in good faith with the union.</p><p>"Reaching this agreement marks an important step forward for the museum and our staff. We are committed to building a productive working relationship with the union and to creating a workplace grounded in mutual respect, collaboration, and open communication,” Anderson said in a statement Tuesday. “As we move forward, our shared focus remains on supporting our staff, serving our visitors and communities, and advancing the Museum's mission of preserving and sharing Chicago’s stories."</p><p>The history museum employees are among the latest Chicago cultural workers to organize with the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Council 31. Workers from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2022/1/11/22878686/art-institute-workers-vote-union-afscme" target="_blank" ><u>Art Institute of Chicago</u></a>, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2023/3/9/23632632/field-museum-staff-union-vote-afscme" target="_blank" ><u>Field Museum</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2022/11/2/23437174/newberry-library-workers-unionize-afscme" target="_blank" ><u>Newberry Library</u></a>, among others, have joined that same union in recent years.</p><p>“Chicago History Museum employees are an inspiration,” AFSCME Council 31 Executive Director Roberta Lynch said in a statement. “Facing some of the worst anti-union retaliation we’ve seen, they stood strong together and prevailed. Together in AFSCME, Chicago cultural workers are winning real gains and raising standards across a sector that long took them for granted.”</p><p>In a statement on Tuesday, AFSCME said the contract was ratified by 96% of union members and includes across-the-board pay increases and improved paid leave for all employees.</p><p>The Chicago History Museum sees about 150,000 annual visitors. This fall, the museum will launch the exhibition “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagohistory.org/exhibition/threads-of-a-nation-preserving-presidential-clothing/" target="_blank" ><u>Threads of a Nation: Preserving Presidential Clothing</u></a>” featuring garments worn by former presidents George Washington, John Adams and Abraham Lincoln. The pieces are part of the museum’s extensive costume collection.</p>
entries.author: Courtney Kueppers

entries.title: Mayor Johnson plans to refinance debt to fix $85M budget hole
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson says the city will refinance up to $525 million in debt to dig itself out of a now $85.1 million budget hole caused by a slew of so-far-fruitless revenue streams passed in the City Council’s spending plan.</p><p>Johnson had repeatedly warned of a $130 million hole in the City Council-crafted budget, but he said Tuesday that deficit has shrunk due to better-than-expected returns in other areas. The debt refinancing will save the city between roughly $65 million to $71 million this year, Johnson said. If needed, the city will also tap into remaining pandemic-era relief funds to help close the gap.</p><p>Johnson says the Council’s revenue plans — including privatized debt collection, selling ad space on city bridges, and selling virtual ads in augmented reality games — have yet to produce the cash promised by a coalition of opposition Council members who took command of the city’s budget process to kill Johnson’s proposed head tax on the city’s largest corporations.</p><p>“Every single proposal that they put forward failed,” Johnson said Tuesday, calling his City Council opposition the “failed corporate caucus.”</p><p>“Had the City Council passed the budget that my administration proposed last year… these resources could have been helping us deliver a better government for our residents. Imagine the differences that these resources could be making,” Johnson said,</p><p>Johnson said that the refinancing and potential use of pandemic relief funds will not require Council approval.</p><p>The group of roughly 30 alderpersons who crafted and supported this year’s budget have repeatedly blamed Johnson for the shortfall. They accuse Johnson’s administration of purposely slow-walking their budget initiatives because he disagrees with them on principle.</p><p>The group, which calls itself the “Budget Accountability Coalition,” has accused Johnson’s team of not following up after initially releasing a “request for information” from any companies interested in carrying out the $2.1 million augmented reality advertising scheme. They’ve also slammed Johnson for being slow to notify the state of the city’s intention to implement video gambling — a $6.8 million proposal that’s still in limbo as the owners of Bally’s Casino <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/12/ballys-permanent-casino-river-west-construction-slowdown-council-members-letter" target="_blank" ><u>continue to lobby against it. </u></a></p><p>“The administration opposed the policy, sat on the required state notification for months, and is now watching Bally's lobby to gut it,” the coalition said in a statement last month.</p><p>Johnson’s team has said that the Council’s projections for 2026 were unrealistic because they required new processes, city contracts or other steps to get off the ground.</p><p>Budget officials also warned that the Council’s biggest revenue driver — a plan to sell $89.6 million in city-owned debt to a private collector — wouldn’t pay off because much of the debt is old and unlikely to be collected, making it unattractive to potential debt buyers. Johnson said his team has reached out to more than 20 banks and received only two responses. A preliminary debt sale deal with Bank of America fell through last month.</p><p>Johnson said financial institutions realized that the debt sale wouldn’t come “anywhere close to producing the nearly $90 million in revenue that… the ‘corporate caucus’ projected,” he said. “This was a bad deal for banks, a terrible prospect for working families.”</p><p>New revenue streams from Johnson that made it into the final budget — a tax on social media companies and a tax on online sports betting — are outperforming initial estimates by at least 56% and 69%, respectively, Johnson said Tuesday. Both of those policies are facing a court challenge.</p><p>Another major sticking point between Johnson and the Council involves whether and when the city plans to pay the second installment of a so-called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/16/chicago-city-hall-pension-advance-payment-delay-cfo-steve-mahr" >advanced pension payment</a> — a policy of paying more than what’s required to help boost the city’s severely underfunded pensions.</p><p>Last year, the City Council pressured Johnson to increase the advanced payment to $260 million, on top of the $2.8 billion required by state law, and has tried to push him to make it in full rather than in two installments. The city made the first payment of $130 million in January.</p><p>The mayor told a conference of city investors earlier this month that the city will in fact make the second payment.</p><p>“I want to reassure this audience that the city will make the second budgeted supplemental pension payment this year. It’s a question of when, not if,” he said.</p><p>Johnson heads into the 2027 budget season after a string of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/04/mayor-brandon-johnson-budget-director-leaves-guzman-finances-pensions" >high-power personnel losses</a> on his finance and budget teams. Chief Financial Officer Jill Jaworski left earlier this year, after the intense 2026 budget battle. Her replacement, Steve Mahr, left last month. Budget Director Annette Guzman, who had been a fierce defender of Johnson’s fiscal priorities, announced her departure in early August. Johnson said she left to care for her ailing mother.</p><p>When asked what it will take to see a less contentious 2027 budget season, Johnson said it will require the City Council “to be in agreement with me.”</p>
entries.author: Mariah Woelfel

entries.title: Recruiting updates on the Class of 2027
entries.summary: <p>Although not nearly intense or as scrutinized as years ago, the fall months bring college visits and commitments in basketball recruiting.</p><p>While it’s been well documented the recruiting road for this year’s senior class is a little bumpy with so much uncertainty in college basketball, there are still commitments being made and visits to be taken.</p><p>Here is a roundup of where recruiting stands for several prospects in the Class of 2027 and some other player movement.<br></p><ul id="rte-e798b6c2-a0a1-11f1-9a65-35dbbbff6c2c"><li>Alex Sirbu of Buffalo Grove has been one of the biggest risers in the class over the past two seasons. The much-improved 6-8 big man with plenty of mid-major interest committed to Columbia in the Ivy League earlier this month.<br></li><li>There is a lot to still sort out in the recruitment of Benet’s Ed Stasys, who has several schools still poking around while he has lined up visits with Belmont, Illinois State, Harvard, Yale and George Washington.<br></li><li>Former Warren star Jaxson Davis, the reigning Sun-Times Player of the Year who is headed to Monarch Academy in Kansas City, just completed an official visit to Creighton this past weekend. He has September visits on the books for Ohio State, Minnesota and Iowa. He’s headed to Michigan State the first weekend of October. Marquette remains involved as a visit date is still in the works.<br></li><li>Crane’s Jamier Montgomery shined this summer and had a flood of mid-major options when the July evaluation period wrapped up. Kent State landed the 6-1 scoring guard who is set for a big senior season.<br></li><li>There are few players in the senior class who have been more productive over the course of their career than Wheaton Academy’s Hayden Schroeder, who averaged 22 points and nine rebounds a game last season. The versatile 6-7 big man with over a dozen offers visited Elon last month and has three more official visits set. Schroeder is headed to Penn this weekend and will follow it up with trips to Illinois State in early September and Toledo in late September.<br></li><li>Another player in the class is on the move. KJ Miller, a top 20 prospect in the senior class, has left Plainfield East for Mt. Zion Prep in Maryland. The 6-6 Miller put up impressive numbers the past two seasons, including 11.3 points a game as a sophomore and followed it up with 19.7 points, five rebounds and 4.4 assists a game this past season as a junior. Miller made a whopping 177 three-pointers the past two seasons combined.</li></ul><h3>New arrivals</h3><p>The Public League has been bolstered by the arrival of talented guard Mikey Woods, who is transferring to Perspectives after playing last season at Don Bosco Prep. The 6-1 senior, who first made an impression as a freshman three years ago at St. Francis De Sales, will instantly move into a center-stage role in the city.</p><p>Coach Marc Howard’s Romeoville roster has been revamped, thanks to the arrival of several transfers. </p><p>The three biggest are senior guard Donavyn Simmons, who arrives from Joliet Catholic, Normal U-High’s Owen Kirby and 6-10 junior Lameck Hassan, who moved in from Kentucky. </p><p>Simmons has flown under the radar in the Class of 2027. He averaged 15 points, five rebounds and four assists a game last year for the Hilltoppers. </p><p>The 6-4 Kirby has been a double-figure scorer at U-High for two years while burying 79 three-pointers for a 27-win team last season, while Hassan is a super intriguing big man and legitimate Division I prospect.</p>
entries.author: Joe Henricksen

entries.title: Cubs' postseason: Who gets the ball in Game 1? 'I want that,' one contender for role says
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> have the bats to win the World Series. They’re leading the major leagues in runs per game. They’re bashing everything that isn’t nailed down over outfield fences. Alex Bregman is piping hot, joining National League MVP frontrunner Pete Crow-Armstrong in spearheading a crooked-number fest. Offensively, this team is — for now, anyway — set like a clock.</p><p>Once shortstop Dansby Swanson is up and running again — any time in September will do — the big leagues’ best defense should be good to go, too.</p><p>But what about the Cubs’ starting pitching? With the horses they have in the stable — including Kevin Gausman, who shoved for seven shutout innings Monday at the Diamondbacks — this can’t be labeled a weakness. Fellow trade-deadline acquisition Clay Holmes is off to a strong start with the North Siders. And the newcomers have quality company, no one more prominent than 35-year-old lefty Matthew Boyd, who was last season’s Game 1 postseason starter.</p><p>As a group, though, the pitchers to whom manager Craig Counsell will hand the ball beginning five weeks hence aren’t an obvious strength. The Phillies — the team the Cubs would host in the wild-card round were it to begin today — have a gangbusters trio of starters in Christopher Sanchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesus Luzardo. The NL Central-leading Brewers, who show no signs of surrendering their lead to the Cubs, have overwhelming Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski and the best team ERA in the majors. The Braves and Dodgers can trot out Chris Sale and Yoshinobu Yamamoto, respectively — each better this season than anyone the Cubs have — for a tone-setting Game 1.</p><p>The Cubs don’t have a clear No. 1 playoff starter. It calls to mind a football team without a clear No. 1 quarterback late in training camp. If you’re still looking at a competition as training camp wears on, it usually means you don’t have the right answer.</p><p>“I would say we don’t have that,” Counsell said last week. “I don’t think many teams do. I think there are some teams that do. We don’t. …</p><p>“We’re going to have some decisions at some point with that, but right now I don’t think I would consider anybody that.”</p><p>But if the Cubs are going to have a postseason hero who drives them over the top, no one is going to be in a better position to do it than whoever takes the ball in Game 1 of the opening series. Boyd, who has had two straight rough outings on the heels of a stellar nine-start stretch, hopes it’s him.</p><p>“I want that,” he told the Sun-Times. “That’s why I’m a starting pitcher. You want the control to dictate a game. That’s what I love about it.”</p><p>If the Cubs have any sort of pitching edge approaching the playoffs, it can be found in their abundance of starter-level arms. David Peterson, Shota Imanaga, Edward Cabrera, Ben Brown and others likely will be called upon as piggybacks to starters to work middle innings, a strategy that has potential. But the actual starters still will have to pony up — in the Cubs’ case, against some legit aces.</p><p>“I don’t have to have a better season than them, I’ve just got to be better that day,” Boyd said. “When you line up against [an ace], you don’t sit there and go, ‘Man, that guy’s had a better career than me.’ Yeah, their track records speak for themselves — they’ve had great seasons, some of them have had amazing careers thus far — but that’s why you play the games.”</p><p>Even Boyd sees the biggest games of the season in realistic terms — it will come down to multiple throwers needed to win any game.</p><p>“You sit there and go, ‘Man, I don’t see one nine-inning puzzle. I see multiple nine-inning puzzles solved,’ ” he said. “And that’s what you need when it comes down to it.”</p><p>Still, Boyd hungers to be that hero. He has seen Chicago starters without devastating stuff work October magic before.</p><p>“You can watch Jon Lester do it [for the Cubs in 2016], can watch Mark Buehrle do it [for the White Sox in 2005], to think about two lefties there, guys that I looked up to,” he said. “You don’t need 98 [mph]. You can pitch. That’s kind of the beauty of this game, that there’s multiple ways to do it. Analytical models might value one thing over another, but you’re still doing it.”</p><p>Before the playoff opener a year ago, against the Padres at Wrigley Field, I made Boyd cry. It wasn’t my intention, but this was a guy who’d been through it — traded multiple times, toiling on last-place teams, major injury comebacks including from Tommy John surgery in his 30s — and being asked about overcoming it all to start a Game 1 brought him to tears.</p><p>Tears won’t flow again this time, will they?</p><p>“They might,” he said.</p><p>Boyd still thinks about his late grandfather — a diehard Cubs fan — and how much all this would have meant to him.</p><p>“The feeling hasn’t changed,” Boyd said. “I’m getting chills right now just thinking about it. My hairs are standing up.”</p><p>He showed his left arm, which will be mighty important soon enough, for proof.</p><p>“All this means a ton,” he said. “It means a ton to do it in this uniform, but it means a ton in general because these opportunities don’t come very often.”</p><p>Another Game 1 chance might be in the offing. Then again, someone else might seize the opportunity with a strong finish to the regular season. It will be a September decision, for sure, just the reality for a team that has much of what it needs to win the whole thing — but no ace.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/24/cubs-pitching-shota-imanaga-craig-counsell-aaron-civale-playoffs-brewers-nl-central-standings-wild-card" >How Cubs’ starters-turned-relievers allow Craig Counsell to make playoff-style pitching decisions in August</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/09/29/how-cubs-game-1-starter-matthew-boyd-can-draw-on-padres-mlb-wild-card" target="_blank" >How Cubs Game 1 starter Matthew Boyd will draw on playoff experience: ‘It’s all energy’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Steve Greenberg

entries.title: Mail ballots are 'secure,' Illinois election officials stress after Supreme Court ruling
entries.summary: <p>As courts continue to decide the fate of President Donald Trump’s executive order restricting mail-in ballots, Cook County and Illinois election officials say they’re going full speed on their preparations for early voting and vote-by-mail ballots in the November election. </p><p>And as Trump continues a multi-pronged effort to sow doubt on mail ballots, they’re also working to assure voters that the process is secure.</p><p>“Voting by mail is not a shortcut around the safeguards that protect our election,” Cook County Clerk Monica Gordon said. “It is a secure, established voting option that is governed by state law and is subject to multiple checks throughout the process.”</p><p>Gordon on Tuesday morning hosted U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, State Sen. Laura Murphy and voting rights leaders from ACLU Illinois, Common Cause and the League of Women Voters for a tour of Cook County’s ballot processing center in Cicero — a day after the U.S. Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/08/24/supreme-court-trump-administration-mail-voting-restrictions-ruling-midterms" >paused a lower court ruling</a> that had blocked parts of Trump’s March executive order.</p><p>The court did not weigh in on the legality of the order. Trump’s executive order directed the Department of Homeland Security to create a list of U.S. citizens, with the Postal Service also creating a list of eligible voters from each state. The Postal Service would then deliver mail-in ballots to only those on the lists.</p><p>Beyond the Supreme Court decision, an injunction is already in place from a ruling that blocked the U.S. Postal Service from following Trump’s order. The Justice Department, however, is asking for a pause on that ruling. The U.S. Postal Service also released a new rule for mail ballots — requiring a bar code on the envelope — but it comes less than two weeks before some states begin sending ballots to voters. Additional legal challenges are expected — and it's unclear whether states would be able to change their procedure in time. </p><p>Trump has said his executive order is intended to stop people who lack legal status from voting in federal elections, which is already extremely rare. The Illinois State Board of Elections says 10 “noncitizens” have been confirmed to have voted in an Illinois election since 1982. The Cook County Clerk’s office on Tuesday said they have had no records of that happening.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/08/20/mail-voting-illinois-explainer-trump" >As Trump pushes sweeping changes to mail voting, here’s where things stand in Illinois</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“The Postal Service should deliver ballots, not decide who gets to vote,” Krishnamoorthi said. The Schaumburg Democrat said Trump is trying to give the federal government and the Postal Service powers over elections that Congress hasn’t doled out to the Postal Service.</p><p>“A federal district court has already found that Congress did not give the USPS authority to decide which voters receive mail-in ballots,” Krishnamoorthi said. “State and local officials administer our elections. The Postal Service delivers the mail, and that's it.”</p><p>Krishnamoorthi said he’s also renewing calls for Postmaster General David Steiner to resign. He has also pressed for Steiner to testify before Congress, but Republicans have thus far failed to subpoena him.</p><p>“I respectfully submit that it is time to remove him because he’s weaponizing the USPS for voter suppression,” Krishnamoorthi said.</p><p>Despite the ruling, Gordon said it’s “business as usual,” and she’s preparing for the election by fighting misinformation at her <a class="Link" href="https://www.cookcountyclerkil.gov/elections/election-security" target="_blank" >“Trusted Source” website</a>, expanding “smart ballot” drop boxes for mail-in ballots and preparing for an influx of early voting, which begins Oct. 19.</p><p>“We always have contingency plans in place for anything that can occur, whether it’s a sudden decision, whether it’s weather, any type of emergency. But I’ll say this is business as usual,” Gordon said. “We’ll continue to do what we’re doing in terms of our mail ballots, making sure that we get them counted, making sure we give everyone in the county accurate information.”</p><p>The clerk’s office is deploying 56 of the “smart ballot” drop boxes at early voting locations in suburban Cook County, for voters who don’t want to use the mail to send their ballots back. The machine has a built-in surveillance cameras, tamper-resistant construction and ballot tracking, giving voters a way to see what happens to their ballot after depositing it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-760000" name="image-760000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/04ff9e3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7993x4486+0+423/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff5%2F4b%2F77f7f21146b9ae5df1acf74bb66b%2Fvotingrights-2608260115.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/774d453/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7993x4486+0+423/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff5%2F4b%2F77f7f21146b9ae5df1acf74bb66b%2Fvotingrights-2608260115.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8f6c9c4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7993x4486+0+423/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff5%2F4b%2F77f7f21146b9ae5df1acf74bb66b%2Fvotingrights-2608260115.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Views of the new drop off ballot boxes housed at the Cook County Elections Processing Center on August 21, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8f6c9c4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7993x4486+0+423/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff5%2F4b%2F77f7f21146b9ae5df1acf74bb66b%2Fvotingrights-2608260115.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8656ba4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7993x4486+0+423/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff5%2F4b%2F77f7f21146b9ae5df1acf74bb66b%2Fvotingrights-2608260115.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8f6c9c4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7993x4486+0+423/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff5%2F4b%2F77f7f21146b9ae5df1acf74bb66b%2Fvotingrights-2608260115.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Views of the new drop off ballot boxes housed at the Cook County Elections Processing Center Tuesday. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Gordon is recommending voters who choose to mail their ballot to send it in early.</p><p>“My message is not don’t vote by mail,” Gordon said. “My message is make a voting plan.”</p><p>Illinois State Board of Elections spokesman Matt Dietrich added that nothing has changed with the state's mail ballot plan, even though legal challenges abound.</p><p>“At this point, it doesn’t change anything about the vote by mail process in Illinois," Dietrich said. "And now we’re basically a month away from vote by mail ballots being sent to voters, so all of this stuff is really coming up. We’re only nine weeks out from the election, so the clock is ticking on all of these things.”</p>

entries.title: The Sky have fallen into pick-swap hell
entries.summary: <p>It’s official: The Sky’s 2027 pick swap with the Mystics has entered fiasco territory.</p><p>With the Sky eliminated from the playoffs and the Mystics clinching a spot, Chicago will send Washington a lottery pick and receive a nonlottery pick in return.</p><p>The swap was part of the price general manager Jeff Pagliocca paid to acquire Ariel Atkins in 2025. The Sky also surrendered the No. 3 pick in that draft, which became two-time All-Star Sonia Citron.</p><p>Atkins was traded a year later for Rickea Jackson. Pagliocca has defended the move, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/03/amid-losing-season-sky-gm-jeff-pagliocca-still-sees-playoff-potential-and-an-underrated-young-core" target="_blank" >maintaining that falling a few spots</a> in the 2027 draft would be well worth it for a talent like Jackson.</p><p>Jackson certainly looked good in the four games before tearing her ACL — 22 points per game good.</p><p>But the current projections suggest the Sky will fall more than a few spots. Chicago’s pick is most likely to land at No. 3 in the lottery, while the Mystics currently are in line for No. 9.</p><p>That could mean sending out the pick that becomes Notre Dame star Hannah Hidalgo and receiving one used on someone in the range of South Carolina forward Ashlyn Watkins. Not great!</p><p>The Sky also cannot devalue the pick by winning out, in part because lottery odds are determined by two-year records. Their only hope for damage control is the lottery itself.</p><p>Although No. 3 is the most likely outcome, the Sky’s pick could fall as low as No. 5. In pick-swap purgatory, falling qualifies as good luck because it would leave the Mystics with a worse pick.</p><p>That certainly would be easier to swallow than the other extreme: The basketball gods could damn the Sky further by handing them the No. 1 pick, which could become USC star JuJu Watkins, only for them to send it to Washington.</p><p><b>Close comfort</b></p><p>Coach Tyler Marsh <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/21/has-tyler-marsh-earned-a-third-season-with-the-sky" >told the Sun-Times last week </a>that what bothers him most about this season is how many close games they let slip away. His point guard feels the same.</p><p>“This is one of those seasons that you’re gonna look back and have games that you just wish you could get back,” Courtney Vandersloot told the Sun-Times. “I think we’re definitely a better team than our record shows, but at the end of the day, you’ve got to win those games.”</p><p>Coach and point guard also are united in the belief that the Sky are still headed in the right direction. Their young core of Kamilla Cardoso, Rickea Jackson and Sydney Taylor looks promising. And unlike last season, when they were rarely competitive, the Sky have given everyone a fight. </p><p>“I think we just have to continue to build off that and know that we’re two possessions away in each game from being in the playoffs,” Vandersloot said. “That’s our mentality.”</p><p><b>Restricted movement</b></p><p>Taylor has been limited to around 16 minutes per game since returning from a groin injury. She gets why the medical team is being cautious but wishes she could play free of the restriction.</p><p>Taylor told the Sun-Times that she initially strained her right groin in Atlanta on July 19. She continued playing through it and began compensating, eventually sustaining a more serious strain to her left groin against the Mercury on Aug. 3.</p>

entries.title: West Suburban hospital owner allegedly clearing out equipment
entries.summary: <p>Five months ago, the owner of West Suburban Medical Center closed the safety-net hospital because it was running out of cash. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/01/west-suburban-medical-center-struggled-treat-patients-closed-vows-to-reopen-weiss-memorial-inspection-reports-oak-park" target="_blank" >He vowed the hospital</a> would reopen this summer, by July at the latest. </p><p>But not only has West Suburban remained closed, the owner, Resilience Healthcare CEO Manoj Prasad, is now allegedly moving equipment out of the hospital. Meanwhile, the legal battle for control of the hospital and its sister, Weiss Memorial Hospital, drags on as lawyers continued arguing in court Tuesday over a proposed settlement agreement. </p><p>Prasad and the hospital's landlord, Rathnakar Reddy Patlola, have been fighting for months before Cook County Circuit Judge Patrick Stanton. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/04/ownership-change-west-suburban-weiss-potential-settlement" target="_blank" >The settlement agreement</a> was finalized in late May after hours of negotiating before Stanton, according to Patlola's legal team. </p><p>Under the deal, West Suburban Medical Center and Weiss Memorial Hospital would be sold for $1 to Insight Health Systems. Prasad would step down as CEO and take on a temporary consulting position for $100,000. </p><p>But since then, Prasad's lawyers who worked on the settlement left the case. His new lawyers are now resisting signing the settlement and claiming Prasad never fully agreed to all the terms of the deal. </p><p>Scott Kaplan, an attorney for Patlola, said Prasad and his team have not been willing to negotiate. Kaplan has filed a motion asking Stanton to enforce the settlement, saying the deal is binding. </p><p>Stanton, who has grown increasingly fed up with both sides of the legal fight, pushed Prasad's lawyer, Howard Brookins, on Tuesday to explain what about the settlement his client isn't happy with. </p><p>Brookins, who has said several times in court he has not read the settlement agreement, struggled to name a specific issue with the deal. Instead, he said he's concerned about enforcing the agreement and making sure Insight lives up to its side of the deal if the company takes control of the hospital. At one point during Tuesday's hearing, Brookins asked for a hearing to hash out a new settlement agreement. </p><p>Kaplan also alleged in court that Prasad has been moving equipment out of the hospital. Brookins said equipment was "possibly" being moved to other Resilience Healthcare properties, but he did not specify where or what equipment. </p><p>Stanton expressed frustrated again. </p><p>"Why can’t you talk to each other?" he asked the attorneys. "Then we don’t have to litigate these issues." </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/04/ownership-change-west-suburban-weiss-potential-settlement" target="_blank" >Ownership of West Suburban, Weiss hospitals would change in potential settlement</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/07/28/weiss-west-suburban-hospital-pritzker-prasad" target="_blank" >Patients call on Pritzker to reopen Weiss, West Suburban hospitals</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/07/11/where-do-they-go-what-west-side-patients-face-after-another-hospital-closes-west-suburban-medical-center" target="_blank" >‘Where do they go?’ What West Side patients face after their hospital closes.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Kaitlin Washburn

entries.title: Bears training camp report No. 18: Bears RT Darnell Wright leaves with apparent arm injury
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down the Bears’ Tuesday training camp practice:</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> right tackle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/24/inside-the-long-battle-between-bears-rt-darnell-wright-and-de-montez-sweat-that-brought-the-best-out-of-both" target="_blank" >Darnell Wright</a> left late practice Tuesday with what appeared to be a right arm injury.</p><p>Wright went to sideline during red-zone work and was getting checked by a trainer. As he walked to Halas Hall, he was flexing his elbow.</p><p>Wright played through a torn UCL in his right elbow most of last season and delivered the best performance of his career. He was selected second-team All-Pro and signed a four-year, $116 million contract extension three weeks ago. He has missed two games in his career.</p><p>Without him, the Bears moved Theo Benedet to his spot with the first-string offensive line.</p><p>The line already is working through some uncertainty after center Drew Dalman retired and Ozzy Trapilo suffered a major knee injury in the playoffs. Former Patriots starter Garrett Bradbury is the new center, while left tackle is a question mark as Trapilo ramps up toward being able to practice in full.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson called left tackle "a hot spot" before practice Tuesday and said he's still not settled on a starter. Braxton Jones has been leading the competition.</p><p><b>Williams quiet</b><br>It wasn’t a great afternoon overall for quarterback Caleb Williams, who threw incomplete on 5 of 6 passes in seven-on-seven work (one of those was a drop by running back D’Andre Swift and another was a heave out of the back of the end zone). He had two sharp passes to wide receiver Rome Odunze, one a 30-yarder over the middle and another in the back of the end zone during a red-zone period.</p><p><b>Dexter’s exit</b><br>Bears defensive tackle Gervon Dexter left near the end of practice, though it was not immediately clear whether he was injured. Rookie Jordan van den Berg took his spot in the first-string defensive line.</p><p><b>Quick kicks</b><br>It was a relatively light day for kicker Cairo Santos, who made all his field goals, hitting from 30, 33 and 36 yards.</p><p><b>Welcome back</b><br>Backup quarterback Tyson Bagent returned after missing a little over a week with a hamstring injury, though Case Keenum took a share of the second-team snaps. At cornerback, Tyrique Stevenson was full-go for practice for the first time in a few weeks, and Terell Smith returned as well.</p><p><b>What’s next?</b><br>The Bears will have a short practice Wednesday morning before flying to Nashville, Tenn. for the rest of the week.</p>

entries.title: Chicago International Film Fest teases 2026 lineup that includes documentaries on Bob Odenkirk, chef Curtis Duffy
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago International Film Festival returns Oct. 14-25 with a Bob Odenkirk project, spotlight on Michelin-starred Chef Curtis Duffy and anticipated films from Tim Blake Nelson and Martin McDonagh, according to a preview announced on Tuesday.</p><p>The full lineup of the 62nd fest, which takes place at venues across the city, will be announced on Sept. 17. Tickets will go on sale Sept. 24, though memberships and early bird passes are now available at <a class="Link" href="http://chicagofilmfestival.com" target="_blank" ><u>chicagofilmfestival.com</u></a>.</p><p>In the meantime, cinephiles can expect to see Illinois native Odenkirk at a screening of Michael LaHale’s “Bob and David Climb Machu Picchu.” The documentary chronicles the “Better Call Saul” star’s adventure with longtime friend and comedic partner David Cross.</p><p>Another local star, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2025/07/31/curtis-duffy-book-fireproof-chicago-restaurants-ever-grace" target="_blank" ><u>Curtis Duffy</u></a>, will be highlighted in the world premiere of Frankie Nasso’s “Ever After,” as part of the festival’s City and State program. The documentary provides insight into the personal and professional journey of the chef, who overcame personal tragedy and launched his Fulton Market restaurant, Ever, to world-class success during McDonagh’s black comedy, “Wild Horse Nine,” a favorite on this year’s festival circuit. John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell star as CIA agents dispatched to Easter Island amid the 1973 Chilean coup. </p><p>For more dramatic fare, moviegoers can make plans to see director Tim Blake Nelson, who will visit to present “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd.” Amanda Seyfried stars as a teacher in an abusive relationship who falls for an inmate while working at a prison.</p><p>Other movies announced so far for the fall lineup include Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland,” a Cannes Best Director winner starring Sandra Hüller; James Gray’s “Paper Tiger," starring Adam Driver, Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson; and Spanish director Pedro Almodóvar's "Bitter Christmas."</p>

entries.title: Dolly Parton, beloved country music star, actor, philanthropist has died at 80
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/dolly-parton" target="_blank" >Dolly Parton</a>, the country music icon whose soaring vibrato vocals, poignant songwriting and sparkling costumes defined her rise from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to the height of stardom and acclaim, has died. She was 80 years old.</p><p>Known for her curvy physique, massive blonde wigs and skin-tight outfits that served her self-deprecating wit, she was among the most beloved personalities in music and beyond — the rare celebrity whose appeal transcended generations, geography and politics.</p><p>She wrote hundreds of songs, including classics like “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You,” that totaled more than 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams. Parton, who plucked bejeweled banjos, guitar and dulcimers with her long fingernails during performances, was a <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/dolly-parton-childrens-hospital-philanthropy-4bceb89b8e6fd4f22bdf96f1861d504d" target="_blank" >generous philanthropist</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/entertainment-music-new-york-7cadef8beead4c236fee89c3922d69fb" target="_blank" >successful businesswoman</a> whose projects included <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/e77b7b4778bd43288890b6c6347e60b2" target="_blank" >a theme park in the Smoky Mountain foothills</a> near her birthplace.</p><p>Her career was forever influenced by her upbringing as one of 12 children born into what she called a “dirt poor” Tennessee family. She started her <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/dolly-parton-children-books-states-program-5aa502c1905babd9604e9b3588942995" target="_blank" >education nonprofit</a>, Imagination Library, to send free books to children in Tennessee because her father, who quit school to work on the farm, struggled to learn to read.</p><p>Parton's first musical performances were in church, where her grandfather was a preacher. By age 10, she was learning guitar and singing on local television shows. At 13, she appeared on the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/37ece4ba776049b896cce5e05f467655" target="_blank" >Grand Ole Opry</a> in Nashville, where Johnny Cash introduced her as “a little girl here from up in East Tennessee.”</p><p>With a suitcase of songs, she followed her uncle, Bill Owens, also a songwriter, to Nashville after graduating from high school in 1964. Fred Foster, who produced Roy Orbison, Willie Nelson and more, saw her potential and got her songs cut by other artists, as well as recording and releasing Parton singing her own material. By the mid-1970s, Parton was a Nashville queen.</p><h3>A key collaboration with Porter Wagoner</h3><p>Parton's partnership with Porter Wagoner, a pencil-thin pompadoured star with flashy rhinestone outfits, was key to her career. She honed her acting skills on his syndicated TV show, and he advocated for her to get a record deal at RCA. Their first duet, “The Last Thing On My Mind,” was released in 1967, the same year she started her own publishing company.</p><p>While their duets were often big radio hits, Parton's solo singles didn’t chart as high at first. With Wagoner as a co-producer, she began to adjust her country warble to a more polished, pop-leaning style.</p><p>She got her first No. 1 solo single with “Joshua,” and reached the Top 5 with the ballad “Coat of Many Colors,” about how her mother sewed together scraps of clothes to make a coat Parton wore “so proudly” even as her peers mocked her for being poor. The song, with its Biblical references and ode to maternal love, was later made into a children’s book and a TV movie.</p><p>In 1973, she had the hit that made her career — “Jolene,” a country music standard with its steady, churning rhythm and Parton's repeated delivery of the title as she pleads for the woman not to steal her man.</p><p>The song topped the country charts, crossing over to pop and later being released internationally, opening up new audiences for Parton. “Jolene” is one of her most covered compositions, including by Miley Cyrus (Parton’s goddaughter), Olivia Newton-John and The White Stripes.</p><p>She left Wagoner’s show in 1974, amid reports of squabbling between the two, although they continued to record together, and Wagoner remained her producer for years after that. But the relationship turned litigious when Wagoner sued her in 1979 for millions in management fees and royalties.</p><h3>A pop crossover star</h3><p>She followed “Jolene” with a huge hit in 1974, “I Will Always Love You,” an ode and farewell to Wagoner that helped her win the Country Music Association’s female vocalist of the year back-to-back in 1975 and 1976. She famously turned down Elvis Presley, who wanted to record it, because she would not share publishing rights.</p><p>Decades later, Whitney Houston’s version of “I Will Always Love You” became a smash for the soundtrack of her 1992 film “The Bodyguard,” and broke sales records. Houston won a Grammy for her performance in 1994, presented to her by Parton.</p><p>“Here You Come Again,” a pop crossover hit and one of the few she didn’t write, further established Parton as a multigenre entertainer and brought her first Grammy Award in 1979.</p><p>“A lot of people thought I had totally lost my mind,” she told The Associated Press in 1979 of changing her singing style. “But I had no fear of change. I expected success, but I was braced for failure. I didn’t care if people thought I was wrong. In my own heart, I knew I was doing the right thing.”</p><p>Parton's other crossover hits included the title song from “9 to 5,” the 1980 comedy starring Parton, Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin; and her duet with longtime friend Kenny Rogers, “Islands in the Stream,” written by brothers Barry, Maurice and Robin Gibb of the Bee Gees. In 1987, she collaborated with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris on the million-selling “Trio” album.</p><h3>Down-home charm</h3><p>For millions of fans, she was simply “Dolly,” a mixture of Southern charm, humor and glamour. But she was also considered a feminist role model for holding the reins of her own career, writing her own songs, owning her content and looking after her finances in an entertainment world dominated by men.</p><p>Parton was open to making fun of herself. When she hosted “Saturday Night Live” in 1989 she told the writers that her only restrictions were she wouldn’t curse and she wouldn’t make fun of Jesus. She regularly joked about her breasts or stereotypes of her being a dumb blonde, but with a wink that she was the one controlling the laughs. In the memoir “My Life So Far,” Fonda remembered Parton's way with a wisecrack, “usually high raunch,” and a laugh that was “somewhere between a girl's giggle, an explosive shriek and a cascade of little bells."</p><p>After her gown split down the front when she won CMA's entertainer of the year in 1978, Parton quipped: “My Daddy said that's what I got for putting 50 pounds of mud in a 5-pound bag.”</p><p>Throughout her career, she embraced her glamorous style, often wearing custom curve-hugging rhinestone dresses and bodysuits even if they drew tsk-tsks from others in the industry. Her look was always a part of her larger musical business plan.</p><p>“I knew my songs were good even if I had been ugly as sin,” she told the AP in 2014. “So I thought, ‘Well, I would have probably chose to look this way even if I had been a waitress.’ I mean, this is my look. I mean, I like a lot of makeup. I like a lot of hair. I like flashy clothes. I like to show it off. But that’s just who I am.”</p><p>She married <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/dolly-parton-husband-carl-dean-dies-2b17ba0e44bcb864a3800bc17afdedeb" target="_blank" >Carl Dean</a>, an asphalt paving contractor, in the mid-1960s. They were together <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/dolly-parton-husband-carl-dean-dollywood-broadway-a596a40fd322f47e5aacc68acc8ece93" target="_blank" >until his death in 2025 at the age of 82</a>. Though rarely seen in public, he was an influence on her career. She told NPR that she wrote “Jolene” about a flirty bank teller who seemed to take an interest in Dean.</p><h3>‘9 to 5’ to Hollywood and Broadway</h3><p>In her first major film role, Parton played alongside Fonda and Tomlin as office workers who rebel against their tyrannical boss in “9 to 5.” Chicago Sun-Times film critic Roger Ebert called her a “natural-born movie star” and the title song earned her two Grammy Awards and a ranking of 78 on the American Film Institute's list of top 100 movie songs. Starring roles in the “The Best Little Whorehouse In Texas” and “Steel Magnolias” followed.</p><p>"I never thought of myself as a movie star," she told AP’s Bob Thomas in 1979. "I knew I'd be a star, but as a singer or as a writer of songs or books or poetry. I wanted to be a famous performer and wear flashy clothes, but singing in movies was not one of my ambitions. My family lived in the mountains, and we didn't see movies.”</p><p>Her love affair with TV and film continued for decades, with appearances alongside Cyrus on “Hannah Montana” and adaptions of her music for Christmas specials, films and streaming series. She also became an author, her books ranging from the memoir “Dolly” to a bestselling novel co-authored by James Patterson, “Run, Rose, Run,"</p><p>The stage adaptation “9 to 5: The Musical” debuted in 2009, and <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/dolly-parton-broadway-52de99e2cb7e47cac2f49bf57ef8be54" target="_blank" >“Dolly: A True Original Musical”</a> had been set to open this December.</p><h3>United States of Dolly</h3><p>Beyond her music, Parton’s most lasting legacy might be her generosity and broad appeal.</p><p>When a deadly wildfire swept through the Smokies in 2016, she held an all-star telethon and set up a foundation that sent monthly checks to residents whose homes were damaged or destroyed.</p><p>She opened up her Dollywood theme park in East Tennessee, a major economic driver in Appalachia that draws tourists from around the country, and established the Dollywood Foundation. She wrote books and memoirs, was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame and was given a lifetime achievement award by the Recording Academy. She was selected for the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award from the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/tom-cruise-honorary-oscars-ae1d8e604d46aae259fed9fdb4e4d4ec" target="_blank" >Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences</a> in 2025.</p><p>With 55 Grammy nominations and 10 wins, Parton is the third-most nominated woman in <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/grammy-awards" target="_blank" >Grammy history</a>, only behind Beyoncé and Taylor Swift.</p><p>Parton spanned social and political divides, through multiple generations of fans, urban and rural and in between. In tumultuous election years, it wasn't uncommon to see “Dolly for President” shirts. But she was strict in not voicing her own political beliefs, often turning aside questions about presidents, candidates, policies and other controversies.</p><p>“I don’t do politics," Parton told host Jad Abumrad on his hit podcast <a class="Link" href="https://www.wnycstudios.org/podcasts/dolly-partons-america/episodes/dollitics?tab=transcript" target="_blank" >“Dolly Parton’s America.”</a> "I have too many fans on both sides of the fence. Of course, I have my opinion about everything, but I learned years ago to keep your mouth shut about things.”</p><p>When the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Foundation sent out a ballot in 2022 with her name on it, though <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/entertainment-dolly-parton-lionel-richie-chet-atkins-elvis-presley-3ede3796031fe13e99bd6b0d74f635a9" target="_blank" >she said she felt she hadn’t earned it</a>, the voters answered with a “Hello, Dolly." Parton showed up to the induction ceremony, performed and then <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/dolly-parton-new-album-rockstar-15f6efbfe89e9370eee4bf71e0ea26de" target="_blank" >put out a rock album</a>.</p><p><i>Associated Press writer Hillel Italie contributed.</i></p>

entries.title: Elite Chicago police unit now investigating Border Patrol shooting of Marimar Martinez, source says
entries.summary: <p>The shooting of Marimar Martinez<b> </b>by a<b> </b>Border Patrol agent<b> </b>last fall<b> </b>is now being investigated by a Chicago Police Department<b> </b>unit<b> </b>staffed with<b> </b>deeply experienced<b> </b>detectives<b> </b>who will look to bring a case to Cook County prosecutors, the Chicago Sun-Times has learned.</p><p>Any charging decision involving a felony would still fall to the office of Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen<b> </b>O’Neill<b> </b>Burke. And potential roadblocks remain if the federal government refuses to cooperate with the police investigation.</p><p>But it’s a notable step forward in the latest effort to hold federal agents accountable, nearly a year after the Trump administration’s aggressive Operation Midway Blitz <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/08/trump-chicago-crime-pritzker-national-guard-ice-truth-social" target="_blank" >deportation campaign hit Chicago</a>.</p><p>Martinez<b> </b>participated in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/10/marimar-martinez-others-file-police-reports-against-midway-blitz-agents-in-new-push-for-accountability" target="_blank" >a “mass filing”<b> </b>of police reports</a><b> </b>Aug. 10 at Area 3 police headquarters in North Center, along with others who showed up<b> </b>to report alleged crimes by federal agents during Midway Blitz.</p><p>Martinez also delivered a USB drive of evidence<b> </b>to officers, according to a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times. She was joined that day by her attorney, Christopher Parente, a former federal prosecutor.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" >Marimar Martinez, shot by Border Patrol in Chicago, speaks out after Good, Pretti deaths: ‘I am their voice’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Now, the investigation into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/04/shooting-involving-federal-agents-in-brighton-park-under-investigation" target="_blank" >Martinez’s Oct. 4 shooting</a> by Border Patrol agent Charles Exum has been assigned to the police department’s<b> </b>Investigative Response Team,<b> </b>according to a source with knowledge of the investigation.</p><p>The detectives there “jointly have more than five hundred years of law enforcement experience, making them some of the most talented and experienced investigators the Chicago Police Department has to offer,” according to<b> </b>the department’s most recent annual report.</p><p>No federal agent has been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/30/pritzker-illinois-accountability-commission-operation-midway-blitz-trump-immigration" target="_blank" >charged with an on-duty crime</a> connected to Midway Blitz. Burke’s office has said “no one is above the law — including federal agents.” But it has stressed it’s the responsibility of law enforcement<b> </b>to build a case<b> </b>before her office can consider charges.</p><p>“The Cook County State’s Attorney's Office is committed to seeking justice on behalf of anyone harmed during Operation Midway Blitz when the evidence and the law support a prosecution,” Burke’s office said in a statement<b> </b>Tuesday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" As of July, there were 31 department members<b> </b>assigned to the unit, according to Chicago’s inspector general’s office.</p><p>The unit was created in 2017,<b> </b>in the wake of the fatal police shooting of teenager Laquan McDonald.</p><p>Despite <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/11/evidence-shows-feds-lied-about-marimar-martinezs-shooting-in-chicago-attorney-says" target="_blank" >early hints of a federal investigation</a> into Martinez’s shooting — including by the U.S. attorney’s office<b> </b>in South Bend, Indiana — Martinez told reporters<b> </b>this month<b> </b>she’d yet to be interviewed by the feds.</p><p>“If the federal government refuses to act, state and local authorities must do so,” Martinez said Aug. 10.</p><p>Neither the FBI nor the northern Indiana U.S. attorney’s office<b> </b>would comment<b> </b>Tuesday. Homeland Security<b> </b>released a statement<b> </b>that referred to Martinez as a “rioter”<b> </b>and accused her of ambushing federal agents — without acknowledging that the Justice Department<b> </b>in November <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/operation-midway-blitz-marimar-martinez-anthony-ruiz-us-supreme-court-feds-drop-case-against-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-in-brighton-park" target="_blank" >dropped<b> </b>the criminal charges</a><b> </b>it had initially filed against her.</p><p>Homeland Security has said Exum “was placed on administrative leave”<b> </b>but has offered no additional detail.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/11/evidence-shows-feds-lied-about-marimar-martinezs-shooting-in-chicago-attorney-says" >DHS says Border Patrol agent was ‘placed on administrative leave’ after shooting Chicago woman 5 times</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Martinez is expected to file a lawsuit against the federal government in the coming weeks. She was shot five times<b> </b>in the October incident, and left with seven wounds.</p><p>“We patiently waited for nearly a year for the FBI or the [Justice Department’s] Civil Rights Division to do their job and investigate the attempted murder of Ms. Martinez by Border Patrol Agent Charles Exum,” Parente said Tuesday.</p><p>“After learning they are unwilling to do their job, or even investigate the facts, we now turn to the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office for help ensuring that the concepts of justice and accountability still exist in the United States of America.”</p><p>Cook County Commissioner<b> </b>Jessica<b> </b>Vasquez, who organized the Aug. 10<b> </b>“mass filing”<b> </b>event, welcomed the police department’s investigation of Martinez’s shooting.</p><p>“Marimar deserves a thorough investigation and so does every person who filed a police report on and before Aug. 10,” Vasquez said. “We urge CPD to investigate each allegation fully and refer cases to the Cook County approaching it like any other police shooting, the source told the Sun-Times. Still, the unit will have to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" >follow a protocol Burke established</a> earlier this year for seeking charges against federal immigration officials.</p><p>That protocol says a grand jury “may issue a subpoena to a federal law enforcement agent who is a material witness that could provide relevant evidence to the grand jury.”<b> </b>It says a prosecutor should seek that person’s appearance<b> </b>with a subpoena<b> </b>and what’s known as a Touhy request.</p><p>The same approach may be taken to seek physical, documentary, video or other evidence,<b> </b>it says.</p><p>However, Burke’s protocol acknowledges that “the federal government, including its law enforcement entities, are not required to comply with any subpoena issued by a state prosecutorial body, and [the Cook County state’s attorney’s office] does not have jurisdiction or authority to mandate subpoena compliance.”</p><p>State prosecutors<b> </b>looking to charge federal agents<b> </b>must also consider<b> </b>whether the federal agents were acting reasonably<b> </b>while fulfilling their duties.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" >Cook County’s top prosecutor outlines plan to charge ICE agents with crimes</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Martinez has said she was on her way<b> </b>to donate clothes<b> </b>at a church Oct. 4 when she crossed paths with<b> </b>Exum’s<b> </b>Chevrolet Tahoe. She began to follow it<b> </b>in her Nissan Rogue<b> </b>and continued for at least 20 minutes, honking her horn<b> </b>and yelling “la migra”<b> </b>to warn others that immigration officers were present.</p><p>Martinez told police this month that, when she pulled her Rogue beside the Tahoe, the Tahoe driver “started swerving into her vehicle striking her car on the right front side,” according to her police report.</p><p>She told police she “came to a complete stop”<b> </b>but then “proceeded to go around the Chevy Tahoe to avoid confrontation and to get to safety,” according to the report. That’s when she said she saw someone “open his vehicle door with his gun drawn, step out and [fire] shots towards her vehicle as she was driving past him.”</p><p>Body-camera footage of the incident released in February<b> </b>showed Exum<b> </b>appearing to turn his steering wheel<b> </b>to the left, toward Martinez’s car. He did so right after agents<b> </b>inside the Tahoe he was driving said, “it’s time to get aggressive”<b> </b>and<b> </b>“we’re going to make contact, we’re boxed in.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/nXGuQ7FrC38?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Border Patrol footage contradicts claims against Marimar Martinez"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Parente has disputed Exum’s claim<b> </b>to the FBI<b> </b>that Exum fired all five shots<b> </b>at Martinez through her front windshield. Parente said<b> </b>three were fired<b> </b>into the passenger side<b> </b>of her Rogue,<b> </b>a fourth<b> </b>kicked “out the rear passenger window,”<b> </b>and a fifth<b> </b>went from the back of her car through the front passenger seat.</p><p>Martinez<b> </b>pulled over at a repair shop<b> </b>after the shooting, was taken to a hospital and eventually into federal custody. Authorities alleged Martinez and another man “rammed”<b> </b>Exum’s car. The charges against the pair were dropped<b> </b>Nov. 20 by<b> </b>U.S. Attorney<b> </b>Andrew Boutros’ office.</p><p>Martinez then <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >began to speak out</a>, especially<b> </b>after immigration authorities<b> </b>in Minneapolis killed<b> </b>Renee Good and<b> </b>Alex Pretti. She<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/05/marimar-martinez-shot-5-times-by-border-patrol-in-chicago-plans-to-attend-trumps-state-of-the-union" target="_blank" >attended<b> </b>President Donald Trump’s<b> </b>State of the Union address</a><b> </b>as a guest of Democratic<b> </b>U.S. Rep. Jesus<b> </b>“Chuy”<b> </b>Garcia.</p><p>She later <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/22/marimar-martinez-chicago-border-patrol-agent-shooting-testimony-homeland-security-congressional-committee" target="_blank" >testified<b> </b>before<b> </b>the<b> </b>House<b> </b>Homeland Security Committee</a> in Washington, telling lawmakers that<b> </b>if immigration agents aren’t held accountable, “more people are going to get hurt.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox trade deadline acquisitions off to slow start as Huascar Brazoban heads to IL
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox wanted to thread the needle at the Aug. 3 trade deadline.</p><p>“It was important for us to maintain the high-end talent that we have in our farm system, but add players that certainly can boost our major league club currently, but also have control and guys that can help us for next year as well,” said general manager <b>Chris Getz</b> four days later.</p><p>Usually, two out of three ain’t bad.</p><p>Rival clubs eyeing top prospects <b>Caleb Bonemer</b> and <b>Billy Carlson</b> were turned away. New acquisitions <b>Luis Castillo</b>, <b>Huascar Brazobán</b>, <b>Brenton Doyle</b> and <b>Joey Bart</b> are all under team control through at least 2027, when a young Sox core might be even stronger. It’s the immediate boost that’s been lacking.</p><p>Castillo holds a 5.89 ERA in a White Sox uniform and has completed five innings once in four starts since joining the team. Doyle is the short side of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/21/white-sox-tristan-peters-second-half-slump-all-star-game-brenton-doyle-davis-martin-kyle-teel-will-venable-derek-shomon-mets-luis-robert-jr" target="_blank" ><u>a center field platoon with </u><b><u>Tristan Peters</u></b></a>, and Tuesday night marked just his 10th start, but he entered Tuesday hitting .189/.189/.297 in 38 plate appearances. And those are the two that are active.</p><p>The Sox placed Brazoban on the injured list Tuesday with a left lat strain, recalling fellow right-hander <b>Jonathan Cannon</b> in his stead. The issue flared up on Brazoban on Monday night, which wound up being the fifth time he’s allowed a run in his last six appearances. Brazoban’s arm angle dropped noticeably in August from what had otherwise been a breakout season, and he now has a 6.10 ERA since being traded.</p><p>There’s only so much blame to dole out for injuries. Bart having his hand broken by a hit-by-pitch in his third game with the Sox is pure bad luck, and the club did well to add <b>Jake Rogers</b> off waivers in response.</p><p>“You'd love it if they just hit the ground running,” said bench coach <b>Walker McKinven</b>. “But we have plans on all these guys, a couple things here or there. We acquired these guys for a reason and still bullish on all of them. It's difficult to make subtle changes--even subtle changes--in the season and expect immediate results.”</p><p>Castillo has reemphasized a changeup that powered his 10-strikeout performance against the Reds. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/21/white-sox-tristan-peters-second-half-slump-all-star-game-brenton-doyle-davis-martin-kyle-teel-will-venable-derek-shomon-mets-luis-robert-jr" target="_blank" ><u>Doyle has embraced swing tweaks</u></a> aimed at reviving his 20-plus homer potential to augment Gold Glove-caliber defense. <b>José Urquidy</b>, acquired via minor league trade a week before the deadline, could still prove to be a useful addition, but has a 5.68 ERA with the Sox <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/24/white-sox-jose-urquidy-will-venable-colson-montgomery-erick-fedde-noah-schultz-drew-thorpe-kyle-teel-caleb-bonemer-rikuu-nishida-chris-murphy-davis-martin" target="_blank" ><u>after getting rocked Monday night</u></a>.</p><p>The first three weeks since the deadline does not represent the final word on any player, especially on a team where playoff contributions in October could be far more important. But the lack of impact has been felt in a 10-12 start to August.</p><p><b>Benintendi on bereavement</b></p><p><b>Andrew Benintendi </b>was placed on bereavement leave Tuesday, with <b>Rikuu Nishida </b>activated to take his spot on the roster. With Benintendi out for a minimum of three days and a maximum of seven, Doyle got the start Tuesday against right-hander <b>Jacob deGrom</b>.</p><p><b>Derek Hill trade dividends</b></p><p>Outfield prospect <b>Dylan Campbell</b>, acquired from the Phillies for <b>Derek Hill</b> in June, won Southern League player of the week for going 13-for-28 with four homers with Double-A Birmingham. The 24-year-old enters the week hitting .266/.360/.444 with the Barons since the trade.</p>

entries.title: Bryan Voltaggio's makes his lobster rolls with a flavor-boosting soak
entries.summary: <p>I've never been to Maine for a lobster roll, but the ones I've had in other places have been so good that I knew I needed to make one myself.</p><p>This version is from my cookbook "Home" and is made with perfectly cooked lobster meat that is plump, juicy, and tender but also firm, and slightly chewy. The trick to this recipe is soaking the lobster meat in the cooled cooking liquid to give it an extra burst of flavor and to rinse away any residue from the surface, leaving nothing behind but sweet, briny lobster meat.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7f0000" name="image-7f0000"></a> (Voracious via AP)</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Voracious via AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Lobster Rolls</h3><p>Makes 6 to 8</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p><b>Trinity Sauce</b><br>1 cup mayonnaise (I prefer Duke's)<br>1 tablespoon sriracha<br>1 teaspoon soy sauce<br>1/2 teaspoon fish sauce<br>1/8 teaspoon sesame oil<br>1 tablespoon finely sliced fresh chives<br>1 tablespoon chopped fresh cilantro leaves</p><p><b>Our Bay Seasoning Blend</b><br>1 dried shiitake mushroom<br>1 tablespoon black peppercorns<br>4 bay leaves<br>1 tablespoon coriander seeds<br>1/8 teaspoon yellow mustard seeds<br>½ teaspoon red pepper flakes<br>½ teaspoon piment d'Espelette<br>2 teaspoons onion powder<br>2 ¼ teaspoons paprika<br>2 ½ teaspoons celery seeds<br>½ teaspoon garlic powder<br>2 tablespoons plus 1 teaspoon fine sea salt</p><p><b>Lobster Salad</b><br>8½ quarts water<br>¾ cup white vinegar<br>½ cup plus 2 tablespoons fine sea salt<br>¼ cup Our Bay Seasoning Blend<br>6 1 ½-pound lobsters<br>3 celery ribs, peeled and thinly sliced<br>½ head fennel, cut into small dice<br>3/4 cup Trinity Sauce<br>1 ½ tablespoons fresh lemon juice</p><p>6 to 8 hot dog buns, homemade or store-bought, for serving<br>Unsalted butter, room temperature, for griddling the buns<br>Potato chips, for serving</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Make the Trinity Sauce: Put all of the ingredients in a medium bowl and stir well to blend. Transfer to a covered container and refrigerate until needed. Trinity Sauce will keep for up to 10 days in the refrigerator.</p><p>Make the Our Bay Seasoning Blend: Place all of the ingredients except the salt in a spice grinder and grind to a fine powder. Transfer to a bowl and whisk in the salt. If you have weighed the ingredients correctly, the mixture should be in between orange and brown in color, and will be so delicious you'll want to put it on everything. Our Bay can be stored in an airtight container at room temperature for up to one year.</p><p>Cook the lobster: Put the water, vinegar, salt and Our Bay Seasoning in a large stockpot and bring to a boil. Remove from the heat and submerge the lobsters in the pot. Bring the mixture back to a simmer and cook for 12 minutes. Take out the lobsters and transfer to a large platter to cool. Reserve the cooking liquid.</p><p>Once they are cool enough to handle, use kitchen shears and a lobster cracker to remove all of the meat. Put the lobster meat in a large container and pour over just enough of the cooking liquid to cover the meat. Let the lobster meat macerate in the cooking liquid for 30 minutes.</p><p>Make the lobster salad: Drain the lobster meat, pat dry, cut into bite-size pieces (roughly 1-inch dice) and put in a large bowl. Add the celery, fennel, Trinity Sauce and lemon juice. Mix gently with a spatula to blend. Reserve the lobster salad in the refrigerator.</p><p>Prepare the lobster rolls: Split open the hot dog buns and spread butter on the insides. Set a large nonstick pan over medium-high heat. Once the pan is hot, place the buns, butter side down, in the pan and cook for 3 to 5 minutes, until the insides of the buns are crisp and golden brown. You may need to do this in batches. Transfer to a large platter and fill generously with lobster salad. Serve with potato chips alongside.</p><p><i>Bryan Voltaggio is the executive chef and owner of restaurants Voltaggio Brothers Steakhouse, Showroom, and Wye Oak Tavern at Visitation Hotel in Maryland. He was a finalist on Top Chef Season 6 and Top Chef Masters Season 5, the first chef to compete on both programs.</i></p><p><i>Excerpted from "Home," by Bryan Voltaggio. Copyright (copyright) 2015 by Bryan Voltaggio. Used with permission of Voracious, an imprint of Little, Brown and Company. New York, NY. All rights reserved.</i></p>

entries.title: Confirmed measles case reported in Kane County
entries.summary: <p>A Kane County resident recently contracted measles, according to the county's health department. </p><p>The resident, who was unvaccinated against the virus, is no longer infectious, according to a statement from the Kane County Health Department. </p><p>The statement included two possible exposure locations: <br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-37789e21-a0c1-11f1-a748-45c4a9a5040f"><li>Kaneland High School in Maple Park on Aug. 18, 2026 during the school day.</li><li>Next Generation Pediatric Clinic in South Elgin on Aug, 21, 2026 between 12:30 p.m. and 4 p.m.</li></ul><p>There have been five measles cases reported in the state so far this year, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. </p><p>Two unvaccinated Pennsylvania residents died from measles, state health officials reported on Tuesday. Those are the first two deaths tied to the virus so far this year in the U.S.</p><p>Measles was once considered to be eradicated in the country. But cases have been on the rise in recent years. In 2025, the U.S. had more reported measles cases and deaths since 1992, <a class="Link" href="https://www.kff.org/other-health/measles-elimination-status-what-it-is-and-how-the-u-s-could-lose-it/" target="_blank" >according to KFF</a>. </p>
